subtopic: SOUTHWESTERN ONTARIO RAILWAY PASSENGER SERVICE -REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
SOUTHWESTERN ONTARIO RAILWAY PASSENGER SERVICE -REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion in a case of urgent and pressing necessity. I refer to a motion that I proposed on April 6 in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications which read:
That in view of the fact alternate, efficient, comfortable service has not been provided in many areas in southwestern Ontario, as promised at the hearing at Owen Sound in March of 1970, this committee adjourn from place to place in southwestern Ontario to hear representations from interested parties for a complete review of the rail passenger service in the area.
This motion was passed in the committee and reported to the House. In view of the fact that the railway companies have applied for many more reductions and removals of service, I feel that serious economic effects will result in all parts of southern Ontario should the Canadian Transport Commission, which seems to be a servant of the railways, accede to the railways' requests. Therefore, with consent, I move:
That the whole matter should be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, with power to adjourn from place to place in southern Ontario to hear representations from interested parties for a complete review of rail passenger service.

speechtext:

This matter is the failure of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to reveal the specific projections of government possesses with regard to the level of unemployment for 1971 and next winter and the campaign by officials of the Department of Finance to redefine full employment at a level of approximately 5 per cent unemployed. speechtext:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: IDRC PROJECTS, COSTS AND CRITERIA
speechtext:
1. We have consulted the management of the International Development Research Centre who report that the following projects have been approved by the Board of Governors of the centre: (1) research on nontariff barriers to trade in selected developed countries particularly as these affect developing country products; (2) a research study of fertility decline in the Island of Barbados; (3) support for further development and improvement of the new cereal species "Triticale"; (4) support for the development and computerization of an Aligned Descriptor List for the use of international libraries to permit a more effective storage and retrieval of library information; (5) research to determine the technical feasibility of preserving food by osmotic dehydration; (6) research into the origins and motivations for migration of slum dwellers and squatters living in eight cities in developing countries. It is contrary to the policy of the International Development Research Centre to disclose projects being considered by the Board of Governors of the centre.
2.	The management of the International Development Research Centre informs us that project support is presently made available only to institutions. In the case of each project approved, the details are as follows: (1) to the Private Planning Association of Canada, Montreal, Quebec, $18,759; (2) to the University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario, the Barbados Family Planning Association and the University of the West Indies, Barbados, $69,000; (3) to the University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, $12,400; (4) to the Development Centre of the OECD (Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development), Paris, France, $28,000; (5) to the Food Research Institute, Canadian Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, Ontario, $6,000; (6) to INTERMET (International Association for Metropolitan Research and Development) in collaboration with study groups in the following eight cities in developing countries, $84,000: 1. Bandung, Indonesia;
2.	Lima, Peru; 3. Caracas, Venezuela; 4. Seoul, Korea; 5. Istanbul, Turkey; 6. Ibadan, Nigeria; 7. Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; 8. Manila, Phillipines.
3.	All projects are considered and approved or rejected by the Board of Governors of the International Development Research Centre. At this early point in the Centre's existence, the criteria applied by its Board of Governors in supporting projects and allocating expenditures are still evolving. It would be contrary to the Board's policy of applying flexible and pragmatic guidelines to its activities to articulate any Arm criteria at this time.

subtopic: CANADA-AGREEMENT WITH OTHER COUNTRIES FOR RECIPROCITY OF PENSIONS
CANADA-AGREEMENT WITH OTHER COUNTRIES FOR RECIPROCITY OF PENSIONS
speechtext:
1.	Does Canada have agreements with other countries for reciprocity of pensions payable to their respective citizens and, if so, with which countries?
2.	What are the terms of each agreement?
3.	With what countries is Canada negotiating to obtain an agreement of the reciprocity of pensions?
4.	Will Canada take the initiative to commence similar negotiations on the reciprocity of pensions with Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Yugoslavia?
June 21, 1971

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CANADA-AGREEMENT WITH OTHER COUNTRIES FOR RECIPROCITY OF PENSIONS
speechtext:
1. No. There have been, however, exchanges of letters between the Government of the United Kingdom and the Government of Canada covering certain areas where agreement was reached with respect to payment of social security benefits in each country to former residents of the other country. The exchanges took place in 1959 and in 1961. The agreements are not reciprocal in the usual sense.
2.	The arrangements referred to in 1. above are to the effect that the Government of Canada will inform the Government of the United Kingdom if social legislation is amended in such a way as to adversely affect the position of persons migrating from the United Kingdom to Canada. In addition, the United Kingdom agreed that residents of the U.K. may be considered to have contributed, under British legislation, to their social security plan during periods spent in Canada. They may then, if they otherwise qualify, and under certain circumstances, be found eligible for a United Kingdom benefit.
3.	None. Canada has completed negotiations on reciprocity in social security with the Federal Republic of Germany, which led to the signing in Ottawa on March 30, 1971 of a Convention under which each country undertakes that pensions earned in it will be payable in the other irrespective of citizenship. This was previously provided for in Canadian legislation but the Federal Republic of Germany did not pay pensions which had been earned in Germany to Canadian citizens. When the Convention is ratified, it will be possible for Canadians to receive German pensions.
4.	Canadian officials carry on continuing study of social security relationships with other countries, and informal talks with the representatives of those countries. As the need for a Convention becomes apparent Canada is prepared to take such initiatives as the circumstances require as was the case with the Federal Republic of Germany.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, without in any way objecting to the procedure we are now adopting because it is our hope to facilitate the discussion of this particular proposal, I want to place before Your Honour and the House a suggestion for the future, having in mind that this is the first of the motions dealing with new departments of state under the government organization bill passed by the House.
In this connection the Prime Minister on Friday laid upon the table a proclamation which proposes to establish the new ministry of state. It was not done pursuant to Standing Order 41(2) so no notice was given to hon. members who under normal circumstances might wish to discuss the matter. It happens that there has been a lot of discussion about this particular ministry. There is willingness to see it established, so I do not think any damage has been done. I would point out to Your Honour, however, that what we are doing is substituting this procedure for action by statute with all the opportunities that a statute affords to hon. members to deal with the matter by way of amendment and debate.
I had already informed the government House leader that I was going to raise this point of order and I would urge him to place before his colleagues the necessity and desirability of using Standing Order 41(2) and giving public notice to the House that a proclamation is being tabled. In this way there would be ample time for members to study it prior to debate. He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the adoption of the proposed text of an order in council for the establishment of a ministry of state for science and technology, I would like to take the opportunity to review briefly where

June 21, 1971
Proposed Science and Technology Ministry Canada stands and has stood in the matter of the organization for science in national policy.
It was only in the last decade-the sixties-that countries first began to consider science as a significant factor in national policy and to seek organizational structures to recognize this fact. As members are aware, it was the Royal Commission on Government Organization, the Glassco Commission appointed in 1960, which first made a comprehensive study of this subject in Canada and reported on it in January, 1963. As a consequence, as early as 1964 the government of the day established the science secretariat within the Privy Council Office to provide a focus for policy co-ordination of those matters which had a singificant content of science and technology.
About the same time, a major study was made on behalf of OECD by a distinguished group of international consultants headed by Pierre Piganiol, formerly Delegue General de la Recherche Scientifique of France. The report of this group had a major influence on the creation of science policy bodies in many countries and was consistent with what had already been proposed in Canada.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to refer to a number of important observations in this report of experts. I quote:
A nation needs a comprehensive and consistent policy tor the support and advancement of science, because there are more opportunities to advance science and technology than there are resources available to exploit them all. The term "science policy" is ambiguous. It too often connotes only a policy limited to the needs of science per se, and excludes the effects of science and technology on the full spectrum of national policies. . . . Maximum exploitation of scientific opportunities requires programs that combine concern for the growth of science itself and provision for the rapid, deliberate application of its fruits to human welfare. That is the substance of science policy in the full sense, as denoting consideration of the interactions of science with policy in all fields.
In 1966 Parliament adopted a related proposal of the
government based on recommendations of the Glassco Commission, when it passed the Science Council Act and created an advisory body somewhat analagous to the Economic Council. The Science Council has a special responsibility in scanning the horizon of scientific and technological developments and is expected to make publicly known the results of its studies and its opinions on scientific and technological matters. In a speech at the inaugural meeting of the Science Council, the former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester Pearson said:
As governments must be pragmatic, a declared and emphasized aim of government support for science is to foster economic growth; to improve our standard of living and our way of life. To this end, we want to know that the very best available scientific knowledge and resources are being brought to bear on problems-new and challenging problems-such as water resources and water pollution; transportation; urban planning and development; automation and employment; public health; poverty in all its guises and ramifications. I have emphasized these practical applications of science. I am also well aware that it would be folly to overlook the importance of basic research. Some of man's greatest advances have come from the results of research that had no immediate practical aim-so some of our best brains must always be free to explore, to search out whatever lies beyond our present intellectual horizons.
While the demands of the sixties were great, we find on entering the seventies that national aims are changing and that economic growth is no longer regarded as an end in itself but as a means to achieve social progress. Increasingly, we regard science and technology as tools to use in achieving our broad social and economic goals. While the old preoccupations remain, new ones appear and our challenge is to meet them with the techniques and the organizations appropriate to them.
In a Review of Sciency Policy in Canada, published in 1969, the OECD examiners critically studied the Canadian situation and recommended, among other things, that there should be a minister of science without departmental responsibility or other conflicting functions.
Hon. members will also know that in the other place a special committee on science policy was appointed in November, 1967, and that it has been re-established each subsequent session. This committee under the chairmanship of the Hon. Senator Maurice Lamontagne has performed a very valuable service. At its public hearings factual information and opinion and advice have been received from many organizations, including government departments and agencies, and from distinguished scientists, not only Canadians but from other countries as well. This committee has published only the first volume of a two-volume report, and it is clear from the conclusions of this volume that the government's proposal to appoint a minister of state for science and technology and to equip him with expert staff to assist him in discharging his responsibilities, is consistent with these conclusions.
In appointing a new minister of state, it is not intended to fragment the responsibilities of other ministers and the various departments and agencies for which they are responsible. Science and technology pervade almost everything with which the government deals

defence, health, agriculture, the environment, the post office, transportation and so on. The ministers responsible for these many activities will continue to carry full responsibility for them, including the science activities which are essential to them.
The role of the proposed minister of state will be principally one of advising the government on virtually all matters relating to science and technology, including notably, advice on how best to harness the potential of activity in these fields to national goals. His policy-formulating roles will be characterized by activities such as advising, monitoring, forecasting and co-ordinating. The ministry of state will not concern itself only with advice on policies relating to the application and development of science and technology, but also with the co-ordination of programs and activities in science and technology with other policies and programs of the government. The proposed ministry of state will seek to foster co-operative relationships in respect of science and technology with the provinces, with public and private organizations and with other nations.

June 21, 1971

As social priorities turn more toward the quality of life, the uses of science and technology dictated by past priorities and preoccupations appear threatening to many. For some, this dissatisfaction turns to condemnation, not of the use of science and technology but of science and technology themselves. Yet these difficulties are not inherent in science and technology but result rather from their unguided development.
The proposed minister of state for science and technology will therefore be expected, amongst other things, to develop and use forecasting methods to try to foresee, wherever possible, both the short-term and the long-term consequences of utilizing various technologies and to advise the government, and more particularly the departments concerned, of his findings. It is hoped that we can thus avoid some of the undesirable consequences of the misuse of technology which have sometimes been encountered in the past. Nevertheless, if we are to make progress toward our broadened social goals more, not less, science will be required; more, not less, technology will be demanded. Our ability to restore and maintain the quality of the environment depends upon more knowledge and better technology. So, too, does our ability to advance health care, education, or the amenities of urban living.
The ministry of state for science and technology will be concerned with the identification of all of the government's expenditures on science activities and the objectives to which they relate. The minister will be advising on the priorities for such expenditures taking into account the significance of these science activities in support of our national goals.
The minister of state for science and technology will be concerned with international developments related to his responsibilities. In this connection, the OECD ministerial meeting planned for next October to discuss science policy in the '70's will provide an opportunity to discuss with other countries the continuing advances that Canada has been making in the field of science policy.
It is our intention to utilize science and technology still more effectively in carrying out all of the functions of government. The route to this objective may not be a short one. There is an ancient Chinese saying: "A journey of one thousand miles begins with the first step." To reach our destination we must set out, and the government believes the creation of the ministry of state for science and technology and the appointment of the minister of state constitute that necessary first step.

subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF MINISTRY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first debate on a motion to approve the setting up of a ministry of state as provided by the Government Reorganization Act recently passed in this session. For that reason we are creating a precedent as far as this Parliament is concerned. Therefore from that point of view this is a rather important occasion, as well as from other points of view.
Science and technology represent, of course, a large field, the boundaries of which are not carefully defined. It 24171-34J
Proposed Science and Technology Ministry
is a field that is not well understood by many of the general public.
The Order in Council which we are asked to approve sets out in considerable detail the purposes of the proposed minister of state. I do not intend to quote at length, Mr. Speaker, but I want to quote part of the Order in Council.
His Excellency in Council is further pleased to specify that the Minister of State for Science and Technology shall formulate and develop policies with respect to
(a)	the most appropriate means by which the government of Canada may, through measures within its fields of jurisdiction, have a beneficial influence on the application and development of science and technology in Canada,
(b)	the co-ordination of programs and activities regarding science and technology with other policies and programs of the government of Canada, and
(c)	fostering of co-operative relationships with respect to science and technology with the provinces, with public and private organizations, and with other nations.
It also states:
. . . the Minister of State for Science and Technology . .. shall assist departments and agencies of the government of Canada in the formulation and development of advice to the Governor in Council with regard to
(a)	the optimum investment in, and application of, science and technology in pursuit of national objectives,
(b)	the organization of the scientific establishment in the public service of Canada,
(c)	the allocation of financial, personnel and other resources to Canadian scientific endeavours, and
(d)	the extent and nature of Canada's participation in international scientific activities and the co-ordination of related domestic activities.
Let me say at once, Mr. Speaker, that we in this party heartily approve of the principle laid down here. As a matter of fact, for some time this party has urged that such a ministry or some other means to bring together scientific policy in a coherent way is one of the most urgent objectives of government organization at the present time.
I want to say a few words regarding the definition of what we are talking about. Science and technology is a wide field. There is the area of pure science which is the seeking of knowledge for the sake of knowledge in the scientific field. This is important and must not be neglected. As the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) has said, and I am paraphrasing, many of the great advances in human science and technology have sprung from research in pure science that was carried out without realizing what the benefits might be. As a fairly highly technically advanced country we have an obligation to make a reasonable contribution to the pool of human knowledge in the scientific field. It is on the basis of this bank of knowledge that future applied science and technology will be based. Pure science, of course, is generally thought of as a field in which only scientists whom we usually associate with universities are engaged. However, there is a wider field. Although that is an important field, the government also has some responsibility to do what might be categorized as pure science in the field of astronomy and many other areas. The divid-

June 21, 1971
Proposed Science and Technology Ministry ing line between pure and applied science is blurred, as is the dividing line between applied science and technology, if there is one.
Then, of course, there is the wider field of applied science and technology which relates to determining how to solve and immediate problem. In these circumstances the taxpayer wants a good return for his money. He wants "bang for his buck," so to speak, and he is perfectly justified in demanding it. There is no point in Canada spending large sums on the development of technology or application of science if the results are to be exploited not by Canadians but by our competitors. Too frequently taxpayers' money has been spent in developing an application of science which does not find itself reflected in an expansion of Canadian industry.
Of course, the government of Canada has a group of responsibilities in the field of applied science and technology. First, it has to spend money on research and development connected with activities in which it is already directly engaged, such as the postal service and transportation. Then there is a wider sphere in which the application of science will benefit Canadians in the future by solving problems which stand between them and a better quality of life. In this direction the government has over the years invested a great deal of money. For very many years, if one includes such aspects of research as that done by the departments of agriculture and fisheries, the object of which is to find the best ways to produce food of high quality more effectively, expenditure along these lines has been continuous. This is naturally something designed to be of benefit to Canadians generally.
There are other wide areas of research which must be stimulated, for example, research into the best environment for Canadians to inhabit in the future. If we are to become a highly urbanized society, what kind of urban centres should be developed in order that Canadians may enjoy a reasonably high standard of life? This challenge is one which faces many nations of the world. There are others which apply more specifically to Canada such as the intelligent development of our great resources in the north.
Perhaps of immediate interest from an economic point of view is the stimulation of applied science and technology in Canadian industry so that our economy may become more efficient, so that it can branch out into new endeavours, so that it can export competitively, so that it can turn out products of high quality, so that it manufactures products which are suitable to the Canadian climate and environment. This, of course, is an area in which the Canadian taxpayer should get a high return on his investment in science.
One thing which distresses me is the relatively low rate of investment in science by Canadian industry itself. I should like to quote briefly from the fourth report of the Science Council of Canada entitled "Towards a Nat'onal Science Policy for Canada." The report has this to say on page one:
In particular, more emphasis in future must be placed on development and innovation-on using science and technology
to produce new or improved goods and services-and more research and development must be done close to the point where innovation will be initiated. This argument leads the Science Council to expect that an increasing share of Canadian R & D will be performed outside government laboratories, by the universities and by all levels of Canadian industry-primary, manufacturing and service.
This is a need which I believe to be generally recognized. It will be one of the great responsibilities of the minister of state for science and technology to advise on government policies which will stimulate an increase in research in the private sector. There is a great field of opportunity there in the way of tax reforms offering incentives of various kinds, and so on.
At the present time the distribution of national research and development expenditures in Canada is heavy on the side of government and light on the side of business enterprise. In this connection, I should like to quote briefly from volume one of the report of the Special Senate Committee on Science Policy where a table is given at page 132 showing that the business sector in Switzerland provides 78.1 per cent of the scientific effort of that country; Japan is next with 62.8 per cent and then Belgium with 61.2 per cent and Germany with 57.5 per cent. I could go on. Canada is in tenth place with only 31 per cent of the total expenditure on science and research contributed by the private sector. This ratio must be increased; more of our research and development must go on in private industry in close co-operation, of course, with our scientific plant in universities, government in an effort to produce a coherent science policy for Canada.
The government must enunciate a coherent and constant science policy and it must fund and support such a policy in a consistent and predictable manner as far as conditions permit. This is a field in which the practice of using the accelerator followed shortly afterwards by the brakes is especially damaging. The importance of science and technology to economic growth and productivity as well as to human welfare generally is beyond dispute, and this is recognized by almost all countries in the world. Yet the proportion of the Canadian gross national product spent on research development in Canada is 1.3 per cent, among the lowest of the industrialized nations. In the United Kingdom, for example, the figure is 2.3 per cent and in the United States it is 3.4 per cent.
Notwithstanding the inadequacy of present expenditures in Canada on research and development, the government has imposed very heavy restrictions on spending for scientific purposes. As part of its disastrous attempt to flight inflation the government has caused the cancellation of a number of major scientific projects wh:cb, if completed, would have contributed enormously to the long-range technological and scientific capability upon which the Canadian economy will depend in future years. These projects include the Queen Elizabeth telescope, the intense neutron generator and a special high altitude research program. In addition, the budgets of the major research granting agencies in Canada-the National Research Council, the Medical Research Council of Canada and the Canada Council-were either reduced or frozen.

June 21, 1971

The long-term repercussions of these government measures will be immeasurably harmful, but they have already had serious short-term effects. For example, the cuts being imposed by the government in present scientific spending in Canada have contributed significantly to the high rate of unemployment among science graduates from Canadian universities. As I have said, there is always the danger that when you put the brake on in a program of this kind you are going to accelerate the brain drain, which means you lose some of the best minds in Canada that have been educated at public expense to other countries, to the permanent loss of Canada.
I urge the government to pay close attention to the Macdonald report sponsored by the Science Council and the Canada Council regarding scientific activities in higher education. We need a clear statement of government policy in this regard. I do not think we want to set up a ministry that in its first couple of years of existence produces only white papers. Enough study has been done by various committees and commissions over the last number of years for the government to evolve a fairly precise scientific policy which should be announced in the near future, even if it is only an interim policy, so that some immediate benefit will stem therefrom. I do not think that the Canadian people want windowdressing or stalling tactics, with the government saying that now it has a ministry it has to start again at the beginning and see what it is going to do. I think we have passed that stage now.
Consideration must also be given to which standing committee of the House will deal with matters that fall under the jurisdiction of the minister of state for science and technology. Perhaps the House should also consider setting up a special committee to look into this question in the near future.
Most important of all, this ministry must give cohesion to the spending of government funds on scientific research and technology. At the present time such expenditure appears to be fragmented. Overlapping and duplication where they exist must be eliminated. The efficiency and productivity of research and development must be increased. The Canadian taxpayer is in no mood at the present time for another binge of empire building on the part of the new ministry. The setting up of this ministry should mean that in the future the Canadian taxpayer is going to get more scientific research and development for his tax dollar than he has been getting to date.
We in this party wholeheartedly support the concept of a ministry of state to co-ordinate and to make more efficient expenditure of tax money in the vitally important field of scientific research and development. This is a field that I believe is going to become immeasurably more important at an ever-accelerating rate as time goes hy.
With those few remarks, Mr. Speaker, may I conclude by saying that having given our blessing to this
Proposed Science and Technology Ministry
measure it does not mean that we will approve of what may be done in the future. The new minister, whoever he may be-and we all have a strong suspicion who it is-will have a great responsibility to make good the very high expectations of the Canadian people in regard to the role he is taking upon himself.

subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF MINISTRY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is, of course, accepted by government, the science community and industry in all countries that the rate of scientific and technological research, investigation and experimentation must increase if we are to meet the needs of the people of the world and are properly to use our human, technical and material resources. We in this country have not been remiss in the expenditure of moneys on scientific research, though many people in this country have felt that we should have done better than we have. Between 1966 and the present day gross expenditure on scientific research and development in Canada has been of the order of $1,000 million a year. Of this, industry has contributed a little over one-third, the federal government about one-third and the universities a little less than one-third.
These figures relate to research done by these institutions, though not necessarily to who provided the funds. The federal government pays for considerably more research than that done in federal government establishments since it largely supports scientific research and development undertaken in Canada in all fields supported by the federal government including, of course, the universities.
Figures published by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, which includes most European countries, Canada, the United States and Japan, show that the Canadian government actually performs a bigger proportion of the research and development work than do governments of any of the other OECD countries. The figures suggest that since the Canadian government pays for more than half of the research done in this country and performs nearly half of the work, the fault for inadequate planning, if such inadequate planning exists, lies squarely with the federal government.
I would have expected the minister, in introducing this measure that calls for the creation of a ministry of state for science and technology, to deal, if only briefly, with our past record, to deal in more than a sentence or two with the monumental research that has been done by the Senate committee inquiry into the whole question of science policy. This committee has made the most systematic and detailed study ever undertaken in this country and has held approximately 125 hearings. It has heard from almost every scientist and scientific organization working in the field of scientific research. This committee has made the most scathing comments on what we have accomplished up to date in terms of scientific research, organization, priorities and direction or the lack of it set by the government. Let me just read into the

June 21, 1971
Proposed Science and Technology Ministry record some of the comments made by the Senate committee. I do not necessarily agree with everything it has said and no person could agree with every one of its comments. I do not expect the minister agrees with everything the committee has said but I thought the minister would make some analysis of the major findings of that committee and put forward his own and the government's views on those findings. If the Senate committee findings are basically or in the main correct, then consistently over the past 50 years we have been following wrong directions and policies and a system with virtually no co-ordination or direction by the government of Canada. If the government agrees with the basic findings of the Lamontagne committee, one might have hoped that the minister in introducing this proposal to set up a ministry of state for science and technology would deal with the criticisms of that committee and indicate how we might do better if in fact we have failed in the past.
Keeping in mind what I said a few minutes ago about how we have been spending millions and millions of dollars each year since 1966 for research, let me read a few comments of the Senate committee. The first is:
Not one of the 100 significant technological innovations in the 10 industrially advanced countries since 1945 has been developed in Canada, while Canada is unimportant in terms of patents or exports of high-technology export.
Canada's dismal performance is surprising since it ranks third among industrial countries in the number of qualified scientists and engineers engaged in research and development.
The Senate committee then stated:
A good deal of research effort has been wasted, at least in terms of economic and social benefits for the country, and Canadians have had to depend on the importation of new technology, innovations or new products developed abroad.
Let me deal with some of the projects which have been failures and how money has been wasted. Let me list some over the last few years in which the minister who introduced this bill was involved either as a minister or, I suppose at an earlier stage, as a deputy minister. There was the Avro Arrow which was begun by the Liberal government in the 1950's and was scrapped by the Conservative government in 1957 or 1958. This program cost tens of millions of dollars. There was the Bobcat which is long since gone. And look at the money we have spent on satellite research. Over a period of years the Canadian government has spent heavily on research and development in this field, particularly in the course of design and construction of the ISIS and the Alouette experimental satellites. In due course RCA Victor was drawn into expenditures, and the common estimate of the total is about $80 million.
The former Minister of Communications when first announcing his project for a communications satellite made a speech in the House of Commons extolling the benefits that its design and development would bring to Canada. Later he dismissed this as unimportant and the satellite is now being bought from the Hughes Company in the United States. No one, certainly not this minister, has attempted to explain the important question. Why spend many millions of dollars on satellite research and
[Mr. Orlikow.l
development if the end result is to be an off the shelf purchase from the United States? This is an irrational use of money. Why now approve expenditures of more millions on a huge space laboratory for the Department of Communications? Are we going to do any better with this new minister? I certainly hope we will, but we certainly do not know that from anything the minister said in introducing this subject.
Let us look at the proposal to build an intense neutron generator. This is a project which would have cost tens of millions of dollars. Some millions were spent and then suddenly in 1969 the project was cancelled. Was it cancelled for budgetary reasons, because it was decided it was not a worthwhile scientific project, or was it cancelled because it was decided that the value it would bring in increased knowledge in the field of science would not be commensurate with the amount of money to be spent?
The then Secretary of the Treasury Board, Mr. Simon Reisman, conceded that the decision to kill the ING was made at the cabinet level. He told the committee which held hearings on the matter:
-Canada's science policy is an accidental by-product of separate cabinet decisions on individual government programs.
What a commentary on government policy! If that was the case when the ING program was cancelled, what has changed or what will change when we have a minister of state for science and technology? The minister said in introducing this proposal, and I took his words down as accurately as I could and I think I got what he said correctly, that it is not intended to fragment the responsibilities of other ministers. In other words, the scientific research now done in the departments and by the National Research Council will continue to be done and the budgetary proposals covering those programs will continue to come through these departments. It will continue to be filtered through these ministers. Is this minister then to be just another piece of windowdressing, at which this government is so good?
Let me spend another minute or two on this matter because I think the amount of money spent and the effort made by the Senate science committee headed by Senator Lamontagne were worth while to the people of this country. I think the scientists and other people interested in scientific research in this country learned a great deal from that committee. One would not have understood that from the comments of the minister when introducing this motion.
Let me read another comment of this Senate committee as follows:
In most advanced countries in western Europe, which are still strongly motivated by the desire for economic growth and affluence, prosperous export industries with a high technology content are viewed as a matter of life and death.
Heaven knows, we need more economic growth in this country, and the 6.3 per cent of the labour force, seasonally adjusted, which was unemployed last month could
June 21, 1971

use more affluence even though the minister is not very concerned about them. The statement continues:
And in these countries the emphasis in research and development has been on industrial projects leading to successful innovations, while in the United States the government has worked on the principle since the end of the second world war that the work done to meet the needs of military, atomic energy and space programs will be done by industries-
This statement then follows:
But the senior government officials who have formulated Canada's post-war science policy expected the government and universities to do all the basic research and industry to take up the work done in government or university laboratories. But this scheme did not work. It could not work. Industry in Canada has not used the results of scientific research done in government and universities, because on the whole, discoveries made in isolation from industry cannot be transformed easily into successful market-oriented innovations.
The committee further states:
The only satisfactory alternative for Canada is to foster indigenous inventions and innovations. Viewed in this perspective, Canada's present participation in the international scientific and technological race seems weak and misdirected.
I could go on quoting from the report of the Senate science committee, but I do not have the time to place on the record all the valuable suggestions made by that committee. I want to deal with what is proposed by the government today in its motion to establish a ministry of state for science and technology. It is a popular assumption that scientific research is the key to an ever-expanding gross national product and thus to a nation's prosperity. It would be very foolish to fall into the trap of believing this and therefore saying that we in Canada must spend money on research and development on the same scale as the United States. Information published in Canada by the Science Council and elsewhere shows that the United States spends three times as much on research and development as does Canada when considered in proportion to the gross domestic products of the two countries and 50 per cent more than is spent by the United Kingdom. Yet the rate of expansion of the United States economy is no greater than that of Canada or the United Kingdom. On the other hand, Canada and Sweden spend comparable amounts but the Swedish economy is expanding considerably faster than that of Canada. Japan spends about the same proportion of its gross national product on research and development as does Canada but its economy is expanding at three times the Canadian rate.
While it would be a mistake to attach too much importance to figures of this kind, we might well ask whether they do not indicate that the expenditures made by Canada on research and development are of a kind that have comparatively little to do with the development of our economy, while those made by Sweden and Japan are closely geared to meet the requirements of the industrial output of those countries. If this argument were true, it would also be necessary to infer that the expenditures made by the United States were even less relevant
Proposed Science and Technology Ministry
to the basic economic needs of that country. I believe the United States is beginning to realize that expenditures for military hardware and for putting a man on the moon may be important for prestige reasons but certainly do not help very much in developing the potential of that country or in meeting its economic needs. Indeed, we may be seeing the truth of this situation today when so much of that nation's research effort has been diverted to frills such as those I have talked about while relative stagnation has overtaken its economy. The percentage of unemployment in the United States is about the same as it is in this country. No two countries in the western world have as much unemployment as Canada and the United States.
We see no objection to the federal government being deeply involved in scientific research and development. In fact I think that is very proper. I could say to the minister that we think this is by way of being a bit of socialism, though probably achieved by accident. But we have no objection to socialism whether achieved by accident on the part of the government or by the kind of socialist direction our party would institute. The essence of socialism is that government activity should be properly planned. Indeed, it is because of the need for planning, and the facility that government operations provide for planning, that government ownership is one of the means adopted in socialist countries. In Canada it would appear that we have a form of socialism in scientific research without the structure and without the motivation toward effective planning that the socialist outlook provides.
There are four or five sections of the federal government that are deeply involved in scientific research. These include the National Research Council, set up many years ago to develop scientific and industrial research, the Medical Research Council financing medical research in universities and hospitals, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, a Crown corporation established to develop nuclear energy, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources which undertakes a major amount of research particularly in matters relevant to mining and mineral production, and the Departments of Agriculture and the Environment. However, many other departments carry on small amounts of research and other Crown corporations are involved such as Canadian National Railways, Air Canada, and so on. In addition, the Department of National Defence undertakes research on a considerable scale that is of military interest, but so far as I can find out has been singularly unsuccessful in its objectives. Then, of course, there are the expenditures in the field of social science which now come under the Canada Council and other organizations. The National Research Council has a double involvement in that it performs scientific research in its extensive laboratories in Ottawa and in many other locations, and at the same time is the agency through which the federal government channels money to the universities for research in the fields of pure and applied science.
Questions have been asked as to the wisdom of combining the function of disbursing funds to universities for

June 21, 1971
Proposed Science and Technology Ministry
research work with the responsibility for performing research in government-owned laboratories. The National Research Council is competing with the universities by directly performing research in the fields which it is also supporting in the universities. That this double role has in fact been carried out without arousing too much criticism does not mean this is the best method because the universities believe there are some functions performed by the National Research Council which could be better performed by the universities.

subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF MINISTRY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the House adjourned at one o'clock, I was pointing out that the National Research Council is responsible for supervising research done in its own laboratories and also for the allocation of funds to Canadian universities for research. The universities have complained that the National Research Council performs pure science research that would be better performed by the universities, while the engineering profession has claimed that the NRC in the past has given far too little attention to research in the applied sciences and to the needs of industry.
At present each department of government prepares a budget which is presented to the House of Commons and, when the estimates are approved, each department is essentially free to proceed with expenditures that it has decided in its wisdom are appropriate. Only the Treasury Board is in a position to assess the relative needs. I mentioned earlier that Mr. Reisman, the Secretary of the Treasury Board, said in reference to the ING project that to a large extent what was decided was the result of accident. There is virtually no cooperation between the various research activities of the federal government and the research which the federal government supports in institutions other than the government itself, such as universities, hospitals, and to a large extent in industry. Particularly, there is no correlation with the independent research of industry or private research institutions.
It is true that there is a cabinet committee on scientific and industrial research which consists of the ministers whose departments are involved in scientific research. But the Senate committee on science has pointed out that, while that committee has been in existence for many years, for most of those years it did not meet at all, and only very recently has been activated to take a belated interest in the scientific research affairs of government. Apart from this one committee, there is no mechanism for co-ordinating, much less for planning,
research activities and expenditures of the country as a whole. The Science Council is a purely advisory body, consisting of scientists and those related to scientific matters in the universities, in industry and particularly in government activities, which offers from time to time advice to the government in particular scientific fields, or as to the over-all trend in scientific research. But it is in no sense a planning body, nor does it have any kind of control as to the allocation of budgets between one area of scientific research and another.
The National Research Council, in considering applications for the support of research in the universities, is mainly concerned with providing support for individual scientists who have demonstrated capability as research workers and who succeed in putting forward a plausible claim for support of the project that is their personal special interest. In almost all cases, the grants are made on the scientific merit of the research with no reference to its relevance or validity for the community, or the economic returns which might be expected were it successful. More recently, the National Research Council has adopted a policy of making direct grants to the universities in support of specific projects advanced by the university or by the university in cooperation with industry. Again, Mr. Speaker, there is no over-all look at which of the many projects proposed should be supported because they bring a more immediate benefits than those rejected.
The National Research Council has developed a vague committee structure designed to bring together the scientific workers in each of the various fields in which they are involved. These committees provide for the pooling of information and exchange of ideas, but they do not in any sense plan the scientific work in the field nor do they attempt to assess the value of the work undertaken to the community. They might be considered ivory-tower committees that are relatively effective in co-ordinating ivory towers.
The great fragmentation of federal research and federal government support for scientific research, and the confusion and lack of co-ordination that results from this fragmentation, is due largely to the way in which the parliamentary system of government operates, as well as the low priority given to the role of science activities and science policy. We have a dozen or so cabinet ministers, each of whom has complete authority over his department and is totally independent of any other cabinet minister, being responsible only to the cabinet as a whole. This means in practice that it is extremely difficult to co-ordinate the activity of one government department with that of another. It is difficult, for example, to extract the budget that relates to a given activity from each of several departments, put that budget together and review it as a single item. It is particularly difficult to do this in the case of scientific research, but until it is done, until the mechanism is changed so that a single responsibility can be established for all scientific research, we will continue to have an unplanned and presumably ineffective development activity in this coun-

June 21, 1971

try. What is the government saying to this kind of criticism, which is essentially the same kind of policy criticism as that made by the Senate Committee?
Many countries attempt this co-ordination and planning by establishing a minister of science, a minister of technology, or a minister of science policy. There is no better method of glorifying and continuing the status quo with all its faults, as has been demonstrated so successfully by the Senate Committee on Science, than by superimposing a minister of state for science and technology on everything we have had up to now. By definition he would have nothing whatever to do with the implementation of the policies. He would not be responsible for the departments that in fact carry out the research. He would be just another ivory-tower creation, examining and inventing the policy with respect to science which would hopefully be pursued by the ministers of other departments under whose jurisdiction the real scientific work was carried out.
The formulation of policy is not planning. Planning requires the establishment of a structure that would place the control of the activity, by means of budgets, in the hands of the planning authority which, within very broad limits of policy, establishes the program and the means of measuring the results achieved. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with a very important piece of legislation, the clean air bill. In principle, the amendment which we are offering would expand the functions of the Depart-
Clean Air Act
ment of the Environment to include a much wider scope than that provided by the legislation presently before the House. When we talk about clean air, our party feels that clean air should deal with all the pollutants of the ambient air, the air which surrounds us.
The legislation which is currently before the House excludes all mobile sources. The automobile, which contributes over 50 per cent of the total air pollution as far as Canada and the United States are concerned, is exempted from this particular piece of legislation. This legislation does not deal with any of the pollution in the atmosphere which is caused by airplanes. This is dealt with under the Aeronautics Act. There is the complete field of shipping, railroads and everything that is mobile. Our party contends that at least two thirds of the air pollution in this country is caused by mobile sources, and is not covered by the clean air bill.
The department has explained to the satisfaction of most members of the committee, although not to my satisfaction, that these other sources of pollution are adequately covered by different pieces of legislation and by other departments. Our party has consistently indicated to the government that we feel the Department of the Environment should be responsible for all air pollution in Canada. This seems to be the logical and sensible way of dealing with air pollution. We would be most happy to have the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), in whom we have a great deal of confidence, take over the various acts and the responsibilities of other departments with regard to this phase of environmental pollution. We think it would be much better to have all these under one umbrella.
We have had a lot of pollution problems in Canada. Every nation in the world has had a host of problems. One of the main reasons for this is that the multiple jurisdic'iions, departments and different pieces of legislation dealing with the particular aspects of pollution have led to difficulties in enforcing the regulations. The best way to eliminate this situation is to bring all acts under one umbrella under the direction of one minister who can coordinate and set up the standards which are needed for every aspect of air pollution in this country as far as the federal government is concerned. That is why in motion No. 1 we have moved to bring mobile sources into the bill. For convenience, we have lumped three of the amendments which are on the order paper.
The amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) will make mandatory the right of the minister to set standards. The way the bill reads now, clause 3 reads "the minister may". We think it should read "the minister shall." It must be mandatory. It should not be left up to the department to decide whether it will or will not do something. The bill should read "the minister shall establish, shall operate and shall maintain a system of air pollution monitoring stations throughout Canada". We do not want the department to say they may do something next year or the year after. It should be made crystal clear that we are going to set up a system of monitoring systems

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
throughout this nation. Clause 3(b) should read the minister shall:
collect, both through the operation of air pollution monitoring stations and from other appropriate sources, data on air pollution in Canada and process, correlate and publish such data on a regular basis;
These are simple amendments but they are very important. I trust that the minister, on behalf of the government, will accept them and bring the whole of this air pollution question under one umbrella. We think this is the only way in which to tackle air pollution throughout the nation.

speechtext:
I rise to speak briefly on the amendment which has been presented to the House. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) has presented his proposal to the House and I wish to outline the position our party takes on the matter.
We are dealing with a most important bill, an act relating to ambient air quality and the control of air pollution. After it had been read the second time, the measure was referred to the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry where it received thorough scrutiny. In that committee on May 13, the hon. member for Kootenay West moved a similar amendment and those of us who represented the Official Opposition took the stand that, though his proposition was a highly desirable one, the object it sought to achieve was not attainable at the present time. When airplanes take off and land, considerable pollution of the air is caused by emissions from their jet engines. Considerable pollution of the air is also caused by automobiles which, under the terms of this proposed amendment, would be among the mobile sources of pollution. This presents a problem to Canadians generally.
However, it is my understanding that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) has, by introducing the bill before us, acted somewhat in the manner of a lighthouse-he has projected light forward to the position he would like to see in Canada, namely, one which will enable all of us to enjoy clean air and clean water. But this process must necessarily take time. We in the Official Opposition believe that the airlines and the automobile manufacturers must be given time in which to catch up with events. They have given every indication that this is their intention. If we passed the type of amendment which has been put forward, we would be placing the owners of automobiles made some years ago in an awkward position since their cars are not equipped with systems to reduce the amount of pollutant released into the air. It may be four or five years before it becomes practical to legislate in the way suggested. A similar situation exists in relation to aircraft. The industry is now trying to find ways of reducing the amount of pollutants poured into the air. While the amendment is in our view logical and highly desirable, it is really not a practical one at the present time and for this reason we find we cannot support it.

subtopic: MEASURE RELATING TO AMBIENT AIR QUALITY AND CONTROL OF POLLUTION
speechtext:
I hope my observations will not be unduly long. Perhaps I might begin them at the point where the spokesman for the Official Opposition left off. He raised the important question of practicability. This, of course, is a matter of judgment. My hon. friend from Kootenay West and I put forward this proposal in the committee as being a very practical one. Indeed, it was from a practical point of view we sought to have it embodied in the bill.
All of us realize that if we are ever to achieve a high quality of environment every department of government must become involved directly or indirectly. For example, we have just completed a debate concerning the establishment of a ministry of state for scientific affairs. This new ministry should certainly become very much involved in helping to determine what kind of environment is most satisfactory for our citizens. I hope I am right when I say we all want this legislation to be effective. This is why the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) should have a direct influence when it comes to determining permitted levels of emission of pollutants from both mobile and stationary sources.
This amendment is really part of a package with the amendment which was ruled out, as far as voting is concerned, on procedural grounds, that is, the one which made reference to the Aeronautics Act, the Canada Shipping Act, the Railway Act and other acts which fall within the administrative purview of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson). I wish to make it clear that this proposal is in no way to be considered as amounting to non-confidence in the Minister of Transport or in the performance by the Ministry of Transport of its functions in relation to transportation in this country. That is not at all what we have in mind. General responsibility for transportation matters rests, quite properly in our view, with the Minister of Transport and what we are proposing today would in no way alter his function or responsibility.
However, we feel that the question of the quality of the air is not something that can be compartmentalized. If the minister, as his title suggests, is going to be responsible for the environment and for environmental affairs, then when it comes to the question of prescribing standards of emissions or objectives with regard to quality of the air he, and he alone, should have the responsibility of setting the guidelines under which that quality and those objectives are to be sought.
The matter could be further illustrated by a referral to the Minister of the Environment who, as some of us are happy to note, also carries the title of Minister of Fisheries. Within his ministerial responsibilities there is, in a sense, a dual function. One of these functions has to do with the setting of appropriate standards and the administering of the machinery to police and enforce regulations having to do directly and solely with the quality of the ambient air and waters of this country, and indirectly, at least to some extent, throughout the world.
The minister's other function is an administrative and policy making function regarding what one might rough-

June 21, 1971

ly term our renewable resources, with particular emphasis on fisheries and forests in this country. So that even within his responsibility as an individual member of the government there is, I suggest, essentially the same division of authority, responsibility and function as, in our view, lie in the division that we propose between the existing functions of the Minister of Transport and the ones he would have and retain if the proposals we have advanced were put into effect. We propose that as one of his functions as Minister of the Environment he would have the responsibility for recommending to the Governor in Council the kind of standards of emissions that should be set, regardless of source, whether stationary or mobile, in any part of this country.
This, to us, is a very practical proposal that makes good common sense, one that we feel is worthy of a full assessment by the House even at this stage of the discussion of this bill. We are very anxious that what is being proposed here should be a practical success. We think it is important, not only from the point of view of the wellbeing of the Canadian people but also from the point of view, in the longer term, of the wellbeing of the people of the world. Indeed it is important, as many scientists have been pointing out, from the point of view of the very survival of the human race. All of these things are in the back of our minds, and our conclusion has resulted from listening to the testimony of very many knowledgeable and expert people who appeared before the committee or have spoken in other forums.
I had an opportunity of participating in an informal conference sponsored by the international affairs committee of the University of Toronto at which was gathered together a group of scientists, constitutional lawyers and others to assess and consider the questions that should properly be before the United Nations conference on the environment. The same concern voiced by witnesses before our committee was also voiced by the eminent people at that gathering. In my view, the net result of the discussion has underlined the urgent need for a coordinated attempt to deal with the growing dangers to quality of the environment in the air, in the water and of our soils.
As we see it, and as we made it clear at earlier stages of the discussion, if there is to be point and purpose to the creation of a Minister of the Environment as part and parcel of the total picture of our federal government structure, it is essential from the start that the minister's responsibilities include this co-ordinating role to give him authority to take the initiative in making recommendations to cabinet, and to parliament as a whole, regarding all matters having to do with the maintenance and improvement of the quality, in this particular case, of the ambient air. This is the purpose behind our amendment. We feel it would be a practical proposal to incorporate into this piece of legislation, and that is why we put it forward for the consideration of the House.
Before I sit down, I should like to say that the standing committee that considered this bill did a very good job. It was a hard working committee. Members from both sides
Clean Air Act
of the House indicated a genuine concern that, as far as lay within their power, they would try to assess the measure on its merits and to make proposals for its improvement. The fact that some amendments have been incorporated into the draft sent to the committee by the House is, I think, an indication of this.
I also suggest, for the benefit of members who were not members of the committee as well as for people across the country who may not be aware of what goes on in standing committees of this sort, that there is some very useful information and expert testimony within the pages of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry which considered the clean air bill. I think it would be well worth the time of many Canadians to study the proceedings of and evidence given before that committee.
While I was in my constituency during the period the legislation was being considered by the House, I did get a little reaction of amusement from some quarters when I informed people that the fisheries committee was considering a bill dealing with setting standards for clean air. But the mere fact that I put it in that way provided me with a useful opportunity to draw to people's attention the point that the quality of the environment is becoming more and more indivisible, and that it is not inappropriate for members of the House who traditionally have concerned themselves primarily with fisheries matters to come to grips with the quality of the whole environment and the kind of pollution going into our waters from the air, such as deposits of mercury, and so on, a subject that naturally flows from that kind of discussion.
I mention this to underline once again that, while it may be some time before the Standing Orders of the House are changed to permit a change in the name of the committee, the fact that there is a committee to which will be referred matters connected with the general quality of the environment is an indication of the point I am trying to make. Indeed, I think it underlines the practicality of the proposal that the initiative for submission to the government of proposed regulations for implementing this bill should rest with the Minister of the Environment, including the setting of standards not only for stationary sources but for the mobile sources as well.
Ron. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment): Mr. Speaker, members opposite who have already spoken on motions Nos. 1 and 2 stressed the fact that the quality of life is important to us all. They also suggest that this bill C-224 in its present form does divide the government's efforts or, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) said, compartmentalizes our efforts.
I disagree with this. I think first that the organization of the new Department of the Environment and, indeed, the various pieces of legislation including the clean air act, which we will hopefully pass today, will enable full co-ordination to take place at the government level across Canada, and permit us to develop standards which will be in force right across the country. In other words

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
we will be able to deal with the quality of life, and in this case with the quality of air in Canada in an effective and concerted way.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) quite correctly points out that roughly half of all air pollution originates with mobile sources, such as motor vehicles, aircraft, ships, railway locomotives and so on. We do have, however, very effective powers at the federal level to deal with mobile sources, particularly mobile sources that travel across provincial and international boundaries, in the form of several very important pieces of legislation. I refer for example to the Motor Vehicle Safety Act, the Aeronautics Act, the Canada Shipping Act, the National Transportation Act and the Railway Act. We have had some of these pieces of legislation ever since Confederation in 1867, and we have had them because they are an expression of the powers that Ottawa has and which are administered by the federal government.
We have recently created a new Department of Environment which must use all the national laws, not simply our new clean air bill or the Canada Water Act which was passed last year. The department will make every piece of legislation a tool with which it can deal more explicitly with different problems. I am thinking for example of aircraft under the Aeronautics Act and ships under the Canada Shipping Act exclusively in the federal field.
We have other areas of exclusive federal jurisdiction. Mention was made of the Canada Fisheries Act. This is exclusively a federal act and, to the extent fisheries are affected, the laws passed by this Parliament can deal with the source. A number of pollutants enter the water from the air and it is conceivable that prosecution can be taken under the Fisheries Act to deal with these kinds of pollutants. Mercury gets into the water not only by the passage of metallic mercury into the water in the form of liquid effluent, but also from the air. We already have evidence in the form of samples taken close to chloralkali plants which use mercury in large quantities which show that mercury pollution in the water and sourrounding soil has been caused by their operations and that mercury is transported through the air. It is not stretching the imagination to suggest that we can prosecute under the Fisheries Act thereby cutting off a pollutant transported through the air.
We have before the House today a clean air bill which will enable us to deal more forthrightly with some but not all of these problems. We need these other pieces of legislation, including the Fisheries Act, although that is perhaps stretching a point,	and the Aeronautics	Act	todeal with	exhaust from jet	aircraft, the Railway	Act	todeal with	locomotives, and	the Canada Shipping	Act	todeal with	all vessels, large	and small and above	all we
need the Motor Vehicle Safety Act.
These two amendments suggest we should amend the Motor Vehicle Safety Act by extracting clauses that were put into it 18 months ago, and inserting these clauses in the new clean air bill. As far as I see it, it does not make
much difference which piece of legislation this is in, so long as it gets on the statute books. If anything, I would prefer it to be in a piece of legislation which was clearly federal. Where long distance transport is concerned, I do not think there can be any argument that it is a federal matter and subject to federal law.
In any case the new Department of the Environment will be concerned with the environmental aspects of many pieces of legislation and will use many different powers. I have referred principally to those coming under the Department of Transport. There are a number of other federal departments exercising powers under federal legislation, including the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
I think hon. members could also have said that most of these pollutants are caused by the burning of different forms of sources of energy. The National Energy Board, when it holds hearings in the future in respect of pipelines or power plants, will certainly be using legislation other than the clean air act, but the expertise of the new Department of the Environment will be involved and will, we hope, influence a number of its decisions.
The Department of National Health and Welfare will be involved. I gather much of the power under the clean air act really falls under the federal power in respect of health. Anything that comes out of the air and affects human health can be stated to be a pollutant, and the clean air act is phrased, in part along these lines. The federal Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, with its powers over export and import trade, can have an input as well.
I am suggesting it is not really necessary to have everything to do with air pollution included in a clean air bill. It is not necessary to have all the powers embraced in one act. I would urge, therefore, that the House reject these amendments because we have already all the legislation necessary to carry out the purpose for which these amendments were designed.
