Mr. Speaker, I may say at once that I am pleased the minister has
Clean Air Act
agreed to go at least part way with the proposals submitted by the hon. member for Kootenay West and myself in these three motions. I think the meat of the point which is to be dealt with in motion No. 4 is an important change of substance in the clause as it exists in the bill at the present time. Subclause (1) (e), as found at page 4 of the bill as reported from the committee, reads:
The Minister may, publish or otherwise distribute or arrange for the publication or distribution of such information as he considers desirable to inform the public with respect to all aspects of the quality of the ambient air and of the control and abatement of air pollution.
If that subclause is considered in relation to motion No. 4 as proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West, the change in substance so far as I understand it, and I hope the minister agrees with me in this, is that the minister is to publish all pertinent information which would serve to inform the public. In other words, the purpose of our amendment is that all the relevant information should be available so that the people of Canada would have an opportunity to assess any action that might flow from the provisions of this act or to assess whether various individuals and corporate industries across the country were in fact following the spirit and the letter of the clean air act. So, the acceptance by the minister of the principle that all pertinent information is to be made public, rather than such information as he or his successors may in their discretion consider advisable, I think is important. We certainly appreciate the fact that the minister has given full recognition to the need for full disclosure of information on matters affecting the quality of the environment and information concerning what is available scientifically to cope with the problem. This is the only way we can have an informed opinion concerning what action should be taken to deal with emissions from industrial plants.
The other question involved in the two amendments has to do to a certain extent with the question of discretion. Unfortunately the minister appears to have balked at this point, because the opening words of clause 3 are "the minister may". The clause then goes on to delineate a number of activities in which the minister may engage, including the establishment, operation and maintenance of a system of monitoring stations, the collection of information, the formulation of comprehensive plans and designs for the control and abatement of air pollution, the establishment of demonstration projects and so on finally down to subclause (e) which is subject to amendment No. 4 and the matter to which I have referred, the distribution of information. So, we have this whole question about whether the minister merely may do something or whether Parliament is giving him a direct command, so to speak, that he shall do certain things. I have listened to a number of discussions concerning the difference in meaning of the words "shall" and "may". I have heard some legal people say it really does not make too much difference whether one word or the other is used. But certainly in the ordinary language of the people of the country there is a significant difference between the word "may" and the word "shall".

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
In proposing these amendments, my colleague and I wished to make as clear as we could that the minister has a responsibility to perform certain duties and that the performance of these duties is so vital Parliament should say the job should be done. We say the job should be done and the government should get on with it. The word "may" implies, you know, a now you you see it and now you don't type of attitude which conceivably could develop within the administration of this department. The present incumbent in the office of minister has been making a lot of strong sounding speeches across the country which indicate he intends to do things. We hope he does. We hope to see some immediate results flow from his activities in this new department when this bill becomes law. We do not expect the minister to achieve any miracles overnight.
Through our amendments we are emphasizing that we want the minister to get right on with the job, to know he has that clear direction from Parliament. We want people working under him in the department to know this is a job they have to do, and that we want them to get on with it. That really sums up the difference between the present wording in the bill and the amendments proposed in motions Nos. 3 and 5, which in effect simply substitute the word "shall" for the word "may" at two different points in the bill. We do not think this is a question that needs to be argued ad nauseam, but we do believe the House should have an opportunity of declaring itself on it. Therefore we put it forward in conjunction with a proposal in motion No. 4 which seeks to clarify this matter of the dissemination of information.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak briefly in support of the motion moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):
That Bill C-224, An Act relating to ambient air quality and to the control of air pollution, be amended by substituting the word "shall" for the word "may" in subclause (1) of Clause 3 in line 22, page 3.
I do so because this amendment is identical to one I moved in committee on May 11 when this bill was under study. In the opinion of the Official Opposition, the word "may" in this context makes the wording of the bill incomplete, since we are talking about national ambient air quality objectives. In our view, if our objectives are to be national, we should have monitoring stations throughout all of Canada. As I understand it, at present we are ignoring two provinces, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, where we do not have monitoring stations. If this motion is accepted it would be mandatory that monitoring stations be set up in all provinces.
When we moved this amendment in committee we were told by legal counsel that the word "may", when used in the context of direction or authorization to a minister, is generally interpreted as creating a public duty, which is a duty for which he is responsible to Parliament rather than to the courts. Legal counsel also stated that the word "shall", which is mandatory in its nature, has the effect of creating, in addition to a duty to
Parliament, a duty that is enforceable before the courts. For these reasons, we were told that the wording could not be changed. But of course that was really the opinion of only one legal counsel. It has not changed my view on this matter. I believe that the amendment has much to commend itself to the House, and therefore we in the Official Opposition intend to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I did not have an opportunity to be a member of the committee which studied this bill, but I was a member of another committee that recently considered Bill S-ll, an act respecting weather modification, which also has a lot to do with the environment. My remarks will be very similar to those of the preceding speaker. In our committee we decided that information should be made available to the public on the widest possible basis. This was as the result of a request from the Toronto University, whose experts believed they had something to offer in this field. They were willing to take the information that was assembled, do research on it, and make their findings public. They indicated that there was a considerable body of expertise in the Canadian Meteorological Society which would be greatly restricted in its operations if this information were not made available.
After listening to the experts the committee agreed that information should be made available to the general public, that any one modifying weather had an obligation to make this known, and that the information should be made available not only to the government but to the general public at large so that those interested could correlate the figures given in various reports, and assess the materials that were being used. In this way the information originally obtained would not rest in a file. As a result, the committee agreed to amend the bill by making one feature mandatory rather than permissive, as originally intended by the government.
I support the stand taken by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). The lawyers who are working for this department are of the opinion that only they and God are able to decide what should be and should not be done. They want the permissive type of legislation. It is about time we stood on our feet and decided whether or not we want to accept their advice, whether or not we always want to allow the civil servants, and particularly the legal advisers, to have their way. As I have said previously, most of the legal advisers are incompetent. One of my colleagues asks me how I know that. I have been here a long time, Mr. Speaker, and have seen a lot of legislation prepared by these people, legislation that was incompetent. On many occasions we had to improve it in this House. All this experience has indicated to me that they are not infallible.
In this instance, I think we ought to make the provision mandatory that the minister establish, operate and maintain a system of air pollution monitoring stations throughout Canada. The machinery to do this is available. All he requires is the money to put it in operation. When the minister collects this information, then under certain circumstances he wants to be able to take action backed by legislation. That is the purpose of the bill. If
[Mr. Barnett.)
June 21, 1971

we are interested in the minister setting up this machinery, we had better decide whether we want him to have the right to do it or whether we want him to do it at all. If we decide that this should be done now, then the qualifying word must make it mandatory. I think the minister is agreeable.
We can play all we like with the words "may", "shall", "will" or "if", but if it is our desire to enforce the decision to establish, operate and maintain a system of air pollution monitoring stations throughout Canada, then that should be the deciding factor. I think the minister will agree that, to some extent, we are doing this now. The Department of Agriculture, as well as the Department of Fisheries and Forestry, have been doing some monitoring. I am aware that the courts of the province of Ontario have been applying the anti-pollution laws for a long time. For example, I am thinking of the case of smoke emissions from International Nickel. Quite a lot has been done about this but if the minister is interested in making regulations of that type under the act, then the provision in the bill must be mandatory. I should like the minister to explain the other side of the coin, the occasions when such monitoring should not be done. If there are such occasions, he should tell us and perhaps we should write in the exemptions, rather than leaving the decision up to him. Obviously, when he comes before us, he must be desirous of accomplishing that objective.
A clerk of the committee telephoned me to say that we could not insert such mandatory wording into the bill. The regulations establish that the legal counsel for this House is the person who decides whether or not these words are within the bounds of our responsibility and I consulted him. I suggest that if the House accepts this wording, then it is acceptable. We should not be playing around with the argument of whether or not Parliament has the right to impose a mandatory duty upon the minister to do something by use of the word "shall" as a replacement for the word "may".
I should like to hear the minister's argument on why, in some cases, he wants this permissive word rather than the mandatory word when he is going to establish these monitoring stations throughout Canada. Would it be because he does not want one in his riding or in my riding or in Toronto or that he does not want to interfere with the clean air in Montreal? Is there some distinct reason why some places should not have this service? If so, the minister should tell us.
We got into a lot of difficulty with a bill to control water pollution which left the standards to be set by arrangement between the provinces. I am sure the minister, having given some attention to this matter, would feel that it might have been advisable to have had a mandatory provision that standards be established all across Canada and then have decided who was to enforce it. Most people will agree that it was a mistake not to establish the standards, so that this act will have to be amended in the near future. I hope the minister can indicate the cases where it is necessary that the estab-
Clean Air Act
lishment of these monitoring stations across Canada be permissive.
The same argument applies to clause 4 of the bill which reads:
The minister may formulate, with respect to any air contaminant, ambient air quality objectives reflecting three ranges of quality of the ambient air in relation to that contaminant and in relation to that contaminant in combination with any one or more other air contaminants that, for either short term conditions or long term conditions-
It seems to me that we will have to establish a plan with respect to a contaminant or all contaminants, and we will have to establish it universally as the need arises. The minister will realize that there will be contaminants which will be rather isolated and contaminants which will be very general. This is borne out by the finding of mercury in fish which does not seem to come from any particular place but seems to come from a large number of sources, not just alone but in combination with a number of other things. I think the minister believes that he had better go into this in a limited way and by degrees. However, if he believes that the department, under this bill, is going to get cracking on all contaminants and that he is going to set up the machinery to do it, then I think he should gratefully accept a positive provision rather than a permissive one in this very important field.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words about this amendment because I feel it is basic to the legislation. I think whether this amendment carries or not will indicate to the people of the country whether we are serious about this bill or halfhearted. While traditionally we are giving power to the government to do something, I think in this particular case we ought to do more than that. We ought to say "Parliament has decided that these things shall be done, so go ahead and do them". Anything short of that leaves the minister and his department hamstrung, without a clear direction from Parliament on what they are supposed to do about ambient air quality. I do not think that is the spirit of this bill, after all the preparation that has gone into it and all the public concern about air quality in Canada. The purpose should be to leave with the people the clear intention of Parliament in this matter.
Part of the Canada Water Act was worded this way. There was good reason for it because the act was vague in its directions and because the government had no real idea of how they were going to carry it out. In the year since it was passed, nothing has been done under it to control water pollution in Canada. Two or three projects of a research nature were initiated, but no action projects, and this was largely because of the nature of the bill and the way we dealt with it. Then, as now, the opposition tried to get some more forceful statement in the act that would require the government to do something about our pollution problems. As I say, in view of this permissive wording, the government can take their time about it, do something if they so decide or nothing if they so decide. If nothing is done, we shall have wasted our time. The Canada Water Act is permissive legislation

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
and so is this. I hope the amendment is accepted and I hope that this bill will provide more definite results than the Canada Water Act has provided.
It is strange that I should be standing here and arguing whether a bill should contain the word "shall" or "may". It sounds as if we were splitting hairs, but there is more to it than that; this is fundamental. It is fundamentally important for us to say that we "shall" do this to improve air quality in Canada, as opposed to "we may do this". We are more concerned about the approach than the words. If there is not a more positive definition of the government's duties to carry out the will of Parliament than is presently contained in the bill, there will be insufficient pressure on the federal government to carry out its responsibilities. I know why "may" has been put into the clause. I know why "may" was used in the Canada Water Act. We are concerned about how far we can go without treading on the toes of the provinces. The government must still decide how it will proceed with the establishment of a system of air pollution monitoring stations, as required in this clause. I think the decision has to be made here. If we say, "may", that is, that they may do it, that decision will not be made. My argument applies not only to this clause but to other clauses. I am thinking of clause 5. I have seen the word "may" appear in half a dozen places in the legislation. I have tried to consolidate my argument into a few words. If the will of the people of Canada is to make itself felt, I think it is most fundamental for the amendment to be carried.
It has been pointed out that clause 5 permits the minister to consult with industry, labour and provincial and municipal authorities. It says that he "may" consult. I think it is essential for the wording to be "the minister shall". Even though other clauses give the minister the responsibility for taking action, it is strange to find "may" in clause five with respect to consultation. If we are in doubt about our jurisdiction we should require that he do consult. I hope the minister will consider accepting this amendment. I hope that problems of verbiage and legal technicalities will not prevent him from telling the House, and in particular his supporters on his side of the House, that the government intends to shoulder its responsibilities and that it is not afraid to accept this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I spoke briefly on the first amendment to be considered when we began the debate. Although I was dealing with motions 1 and 8, I will not repeat the points I made. I understand motion No. 4 is to be accepted by the government. I should like to deal rather briefly, if I may, with motion No. 5 dealing with the formulation of air quality objectives. This is a very important clause of the bill. In setting up air quality objectives, as outlined under clause 4, we shall stipulate several different ranges of air quality throughout Canada. We find that there is to be the tolerable range, the acceptable range and the desirable range. Everybody knows that industry will aim for the tolerable range. That does not make me happy, because I
think we should set high standards, and force industry and those polluting our environment to meet those high standards. This is our objective in trying to get polluting industries to clean up. We want to live in a decent environment and breathe clean air. That is why I endorse what other speakers have said and that is why the provision must be mandatory.
The legislation provides that the minister "may" formulate certain standards with respect to air contaminants. The motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) says that the minister "shall formulate with respect to all air contaminants...". It would be mandatory in effect. We do not want to leave this matter to the discretion of some departmental official or to the discretion of the minister. We do not want them to say "we will set certain standards for certain areas," because later we will find that we do not have national standards for air contaminants. The operation of this provision will be extremely limited indeed. That is why there must be this change in wording. I urge the minister to accept this amendment because it would be a step forward and would tighten the legislation. Accepting it would convince the Canadian people that we are out to do a good job in cleaning up the environment. I think that this mandatory provision must be in the legislation. If it is not, there will be a lot of manoeuvring around. If you do not accept the amendment, some lawyer wil be turned loose in the courts and he will find all the excuses in the world as to why action should not be taken. I suggest that the minister accept this amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we, on the government side, are prepared to accept motion No. 4. We contest motions 3 and 5. However, we would not like you or members of the House to think that we oppose motions 3 and 5 for lack of concern about the problem of air pollution. I must rely on the advice I have been given by law officers of the Crown who were seconded to my department from the Department of Justice. They have been consistent in recent years in interpreting Canadian legislation and, as a nonlawyer, I do not wish to question their advice in this connection. They use the word "may" rather differently than most of us do in everyday conversation. They use it, implying an obligation, a very serious obligation. The obligation is on the minister. The minister has a public duty, which I am certainly prepared to accept and which I am sure all future ministers of the environment will be prepared to accept, to act in certain ways which are outlined in the bill. This is a duty which will be enforced by Parliament.
The word "shall" differs, implying mandatory action enforceable through the courts. It is a question of whom the minister must regard as his master or, to put it another way, who the real master of the minister is. Is it to be Parliament or the courts? If, in the last analysis, his master is the courts, then our draftsmen use "shall". But if it is Parliament, then "may" has real significance and is binding on the minister.

June 21, 1971

We are dealing with a major part of the bill which is headed "Research, Information, Data Collection and Establishment of National Ambient Air Quality Objectives". The present wording of Bill C-224 reads:
The Minister may,
(a)	establish, operate and maintain a system of air pollution monitoring stations throughout Canada;
(b)	collect... data . ..
(c)	conduct research . . .
(d)	formulate comprehensive plans...
(e)	publish or otherwise distribute ... information-
As I understand it, the minister is required by Parliament to do all these things, even though the text says "may". The legal interpretation is that he must do these things, his master being Parliament, not the courts. That is my layman's interpretation of the legal advice which I have received. As a non-lawyer this particular interpretation should not be taken too literally.
Dealing specifically with amendment No. 3, the word "shall' is offered as a substitute for the word "may". If the amendment is accepted, the minister shall do all these things. In other words, the minister is required by the courts to do all these things. As the bill presently reads, the minister is required by Parliament to do them. Personally, I would settle for Parliament rather than the courts. I urge the House to reject amendment No. 3.
The government is prepared to accept motion No. 4. It is prepared to accept the amendment which states that all the pertinent information, that is all information gathered by research monitoring stations, which would serve to inform the public in respect to all aspects of the quality of the ambient air, be made available to the public. As such it is an acceptable amendment.
Amendment No. 5 not only involves substitution of the word "shall" for the word "may", but gets us a little further into the nature of the bill. This is a technical matter. It is our intention to promulgate air quality objectives for a wide range of air contaminants. Objectives are not standards. Objectives are described in ranges.
Another part of the bill deals with precise standards, for example standards of emission and, more specifically, standards at the chimney top. I do not believe that the Canadian government should be promulgating air quality objectives for certain air contaminants. In other words, there are certain air contaminants which are so lethal that we should not be talking about ranges at all. We should not talk about any degree of uncertainty. We should talk about concentrations of the precise order of zero-or very close to zero. Therefore, I would not want to see the word "all" or the phrase "all air contaminants" in respect of this technical matter of air quality objectives. To put it another way, we can promulgate air quality objectives for the not so lethal and not so serious air contaminants. But we cannot play around with certain very hazardous substances. We should not talk about ranges in their case. Instead of the word "all", we should retain the word "any" which implies most contaminants
which are not as serious as others and not rule out the possibility of our declaring specific standards for certain lethal substances.

The Prime Minister, then Minister of Justice, looked us straight in the eye and said that the government was the master of Parliament. This bill is replete with the words "may" and "shall". In other words, dealing with higher authority, the minister is

compelled to make a recommendation. He shall take certain things into consideration.
I did not have time to make an exhaustive study, but I believe that is the only place the word "shall" is used. The rest of the bill is permissive. On practically every other page of the bill, there is a suggestion that the minister may do something, but when it comes to a direction to the citizen, the word "shall" is used. Page 6 has been called to my attention. I quote:
The operator of any work, undertaking or business the operation of which the Minister has reasonable grounds to believe results in the emission into the ambient air of an air contaminant, shall,-
There is no question about it; "shall" is mandatory. He has to do it. Clause 9, subclause (2) reads:

Mr. Speaker, the two motions which we are now discussing, Nos. 6 and 11, deal with what we think is a very important aspect of pollution in Canada, namely allowing the general public to lodge complaints and to be more effective in bringing serious cases of pollution to the attention of the minister in the hope that some action will be taken to clean them up.
I should like to deal with motion No. 6 first. The motion seeks to add a subclause to clause 5 in these terms:
If any six persons lodge a complaint with the Minister concerning any aspect of the quality of the ambient air or of the quantity and concentration of air contaminants, the Minister shall establish a Commission of Inquiry for the purpose of con-

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
ducting a public hearing at which the ambient air quality objectives and the national emission standards shall be reviewed.
Even today, a large number of complaints from all parts of Canada are being made about air pollution. As the bill is presently constituted, there is no effective means whereby groups of interested citizens or organizations can get action taken, or can force the government to take action, to deal with serious cases of air pollution. In framing the legislation, all aspects of bringing such problems to the attention of the government should be examined. Under the bill there is going to be co-operation between the various provinces on pollution matters, and there is no doubt that a host of problems will be encountered that are going to be overlooked by the department in charge. For example, there might be a serious air pollution problem in a particular area but the municipality or the people in the area may be reluctant to make representations to the industry causing the pollution for fear the industry might close down, leave the district and lay off its workers. In my view, no industry in Canada has the right to pollute the air to the point where a great deal of discomfort is caused to the people of the area, the aesthetic values of life are detrimentally affected, and the people become fed up and look for some kind of redress.
I expect the minister will tell me that there are clauses in the bill that will enable us to go after such companies. However, these provisions are very vague, whereas my amendment is clear and concise. If six individuals lodge a complaint, a sensible complaint backed with facts and figures, then the minister must look into the complaint. I can give you an excellent example. Just across the river from us there is a pulp mill. If the odours from that mill are inconveniencing a large number of people in this area, possibly causing health problems, while they might not be classed as a significant danger, we should be in a position to tackle that problem. People should be able to bring to the attention of the minister such situations and ask that a check be made to find out the percentage of hydrogen-sulphide emitted from those stacks. In this way they could find whether it was too high, and could get action from industries currently contaminating our environment.
I do not think there is much more I can add. A number of hon. members would like to say a few words about these amendments. I feel these amendments would materially strengthen the bill, and I urge the minister to accept them.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks in favour of this amendment. There should be a means whereby people in any locality can be heard if they find circumstances objectionable and have cause to believe they have a complaint. This provision would prove much more effective than the regulations that have been in effect, in recent years. A good example of how this provision would work was recently seen in southern Ontario. There was a complaint that a certain plant was poisoning the atmosphere, making the people sick and affecting their farm operations. As a result, a television crew went to the area and produced an expose. Eventually, there was an investigation by the provincial government. The question immediately arises as to whether the CBC or the CTV was seeking publicity or whether the people concerned had a valid complaint. At the present time, people have no way of instigating an investigation.
The previous speaker was asked whether this amendment would have the effect of creating a multitude of investigations. Surely, it is generally known that the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission operates under a provision which allows six people to request an investigation when they believe there is a combine causing excessive price fixing, or in some way adversely affecting the people concerned. Such a practice is not as serious as a situation which pollutes the atmosphere these people must breathe. People can survive adverse economic conditions, but they may not survive pollution.
This government has decided to introduce legislation prohibiting the advertising of cigarettes. I can decide whether I smoke cigarettes. The government, in its wisdom, believes cigarette-smoking is injurious and is taking upon itself the obligation to introduce legislation to prohibit such advertisements in certain publications, on television and on radio. If a plant is polluting the air, the individual in the local area cannot decide to stop breathing. If you walk in the halls of this building and smell an odour of rotten eggs, you know that it comes from the plant across the river. However, you do not have a choice as to whether or not you should breathe the air. There is no other air to breathe.
This amendment suggests that when six people consider the air they breathe to be polluted and unfit, or that it

June 21, 1971

may cause damage to their animals or their environment, indeed even the vegetation around them, they can lodge a complaint. I do not think ordinary people would undertake such action lightly, but would only do so when they considered there was a danger to their lives and their environment. I cannot see why the government should not accept such an amendment. In this way they could show their willingness to give any six people the opportunity of requesting an investigation. The terms and conditions could be set out as they are for the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission.
This is a government which advocates participatory democracy. Such an avenue through which individuals could participate would be welcome. Imagine all the people who could participate. Any six people anywhere could be a participating part of the total. That is a very intriguing idea, and this is what this amendment offers. I seriously feel it should be adopted. We could very well find instances in which a situation could be checked in its early stages by reason of complaints from the people who live in the area. A very considerable amount of damage may be done before some group of people is forced to bring a lawsuit or forced to try to get some publicity in respect of a situation which has become intolerable.

Mr. Speaker, I was very anxious to become involved in this discussion because this is a matter which very seriously affects my own constituency, and indeed the whole of the city of Toronto. A very serious air pollution problem exists there. This particular amendment is designed to secure active participation. Indeed the whole of clause 5 is designed to secure the active participation of the people themselves in the enforcement of this legislation. I say that nothing is more important to the minister in carrying out the duties he has embarked upon than to arouse the interest and concern of the local people in order to have them participate in reviewing the conditions which exist and then participate in the enforcement of the law when it has been determined there has been some breach of the law. The problem of enforcement is of importance. One reason is that the people who are doing the polluting often are the most powerful organization in the whole community.
A local organization in my constituency of active and interested citizens, for WARD-9, has a pollution task force. I shall ask the minister to later confer with these people because they have done a tremendous job in investigating the sources of air pollution and other forms of pollution in the Toronto area. Their preliminary findings are the following: The three main plants in the area are the Richard L. Hearn generating station of Ontario Hydro, the municipal incinerator on Commissioners street, operated by the Metro Works Department, and the main sewage treatment plant on Ashbridge's Bay, also operated by the Metro Works Department. What have these three public bodies been doing? They have polluted the air of the residents of that area. The Hearn Plant is a big source of pollution and a highly visible one. Changes are being made in that plant but the problem remains. The
Clean Air Act
Commissioners Street incinerator is the largest in the city. Although it gets less attention than the Hearn plant, it causes serious local problems. Odours, fly ash and black smoke are regularly emitted from its three stacks. The plant is frequently used to bum many more tons of garbage a day than it was designed to handle. This is illegal but nobody has done anything about it. The average person does not feel in a position to proceed against a large municipal institution of that sort. The main sewage treatment plan on Ashbridge's Bay, operated by the Metro Works Department, is the source of at least three different kinds of pollution. Smoke is regularly emitted in large amounts from some or all of the four stacks. Foul and highly offensive smells blow from the aeration tanks and sludge lagoons at the plant to residential areas to the north and east. Raw sewage goes through the plant into the lake. All three kinds of pollution call for immediate attention and control.
These are the view of a responsible body of citizens in this particular area. They point out the need for the type of enforcement this amendment envisages. Amendment No. 6 proposes that if any six persons lodge a complaint then an inquiry must be made. This is modelled, as I believe most members will know, on the Combines Investigation Act which provides that the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act can be set in operation when enough people make a complaint. I suggest that this is very essential in this case. It is true that under clause 5 as proposed the minister is, in my view, required to consult with-and I am sure he intends to do so-and organize conferences of, representatives of industry and labour, provincial and municipal authorities and other persons interested in any aspect of the quality of the ambient air or of the control or abatement of air pollution. So, the minister is to consult. Well, and good. I hope he will do so and I promise him the co-operation of the people in my constituency.
The next point has to do with the setting up of committees. That is an excellent idea. But now my friend has submitted an amendment which adds a necessary ingredient. Suppose the minister should be politically embarrassed to take action against the Metro Works Department of the city of Toronto or should be embarrassed to pursue an action against Ontario Hydro? If this amendment were incorporated in the legislation a public inquiry instituted by this government would be part of the proceedings and this would enable the matter to be aired and the complaints sifted in order to determine whether or not the law had been broken. If it had been broken, one would assume that merely because of the embarrassment involved the public body would make plans to cease and desist polluting the air of the area in question.
I think I have made the point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, on this. I say again to the minister that we wish him every possible success in his endeavours to make this legislation effective and to genuinely take action to enable the people who may be involved to institute an inquiry if they should find that no adequate action is being taken. Therefore, I support the amendment and urge the House to accept it.

Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting amendment moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding). It is somewhat similar to discussions which took place when the bill was before the committee. The amendment reads as follows:
If any six persons lodge a complaint with the Minister concerning any aspect of the quality of the ambient air or of the quantity and concentration of air contaminants, the Minister shall establish a Commission of Inquiry for the purpose of conducting a public hearing at which the ambient air quality objectives and the national emission standards shall be reviewed.
It is suggested that this paragraph be added to clause 5 immediately after line 4 at page 6. So, for the benefit of members and Hansard, I believe it would be advisable to place on record the wording of clause 5, which deals with consultation. We find these words:
(1)	In carrying out his responsibilities under this Act the Minister may consult with, and organize conferences of, representatives of industry and labour, provincial and municipal authorities and other persons interested in any aspect of the quality of the ambient air or of the control or abatement of air pollution.
(2)	The Governor in Council may establish advisory and other committees to advise or assist the Minister or to perforin such duties in relation to the control and abatement of air pollution and the coordination of the activities of governments, institutions and persons in relation thereto as the Governor in Council may specify, and may fix or determine the remuneration and expenses, if any, to be paid to the members of any committees so established.
In view of the wording in the bill and in the amendment, Mr. Speaker, I personally feel there is some conflict here. There may well be some redundacy in the amendment as moved. It is quite evident that pollution is a national problem. In a few generations Canada's national heritage of rich soil, clear skies, crystal lakes and inviting rivers will come under the threat of deterioration from our present municipal sewage systems. I will give full credit to the minister for his efforts to bring the problem into focus. It is a problem that has become acute in many geographic areas.
We have seen an example of this in the province of New Brunswick, where it became an international problem. One of our rivers became polluted because of activities in the United States, so the citizens of New Brunswick found it necessary to build a dam to keep pollution from the American side from coming into that river. A plant in Newfoundland which discharged phosphorus into the ocean destroyed large quantities of fish. As I say, I give the minister credit for highlighting the pollution problems in Canada.
There is a growing demand today for clean air, clean soil and pure water, all of them vital to our health and wealth, and to the enjoyment of our national environment. It is evident from the amendments that have been moved to Bill C-224 that this problem has become complex. It is a very difficult one. It will not be solved easily and quickly. It will not be solved without the expenditure of vast sums of money. This leads me to question the amendment, and I hope there will be further debate on it, because I question whether it would be desirable to
have a provision permitting any six persons to lodge a complaint with the minister concerning the quality of ambient air, which would require him to establish a commission of inquiry.
The words used are that the minister "shall establish a commission of inquiry." This afternoon we have had quite a debate on the usage of the words "may" and "shall." If the word may had been included in this amendment I would have its meaning clearer in my mind, but I feel that to tie the minister down to setting up a commission of inquiry if six people lodge a complaint about a certain quality of air is a little bit too constrictive. In my view we must do something about controlling pollution, but controlling pollution is something that must be done under a system of priorities. We must establish certain priorities and certain goals that are desirable for society. Technology exists to enable us to establish acceptable levels of pollution, but a value judgment has to be made, and then society has to decide whether or not it is worthwhile to spend the money that is required to achieve a desired end.
I make these few comments on this amendment hoping that others will be able to give a little better interpretation of what the amendment really means. Six people may well lodge a complaint, but it may be an irresponsible complaint which would create a vast expenditure of public funds that in the end would not lead to any desirable change in the situation. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I have some doubts about the amendment, but I am willing to listen to further argument.

Mr. Speaker, the proposal in question is drawn from what used to be a section in the old Combines Investigations Act, and which I find is no longer there. It has been taken out of that act. The people who love participatory democracy only want this participation to go to a certain level. When it gets below that level, they don't want participation. However, let us look at what was in the Combines Investigations Act for the purpose of determining whether or not we can accept this proposal. There are quite a number of points of similarity.
Section 7 of the old Combines Act provided that:
Any six persons, Canadian citizens, resident in Canada, of the full age of twenty-one years, who are of the opinion that an offence has been or is being committed-
You could put that side by side with what is being proposed here in the amendment now under consideration:
If any six persons lodge a complaint with the Minister concerning any aspect of the quality of the ambient air ...
Obviously, the complaint under the Combines Act had to do with the quality of the competition with regard to certain phases of economic activity. Here, the complaint is with respect to an aspect of the quality of the ambient air. The Combines Investigations Act went on to say:
-an offence has been or is being committed-

Then, under certain sections of that act or of the Criminal Code,
-may apply to the Director for an inquiry into such matter, and shall place before the Director the evidence on which such opinion is based.
To that extent, there seems to be quite a similarity, but the Combines Act then went on to say:
The application shall be accompanied by a statement in the form of a solemn or statutory declaration showing
(a) the names and addresses of the applicants-
The names and addresses of those applicants and so on, and also
-the nature of the alleged offence and the names of the persons believed to be concerned therein and privy thereto; and, if the application relates to an offence against section 32, the manner in which, and where possible the extent to which, the alleged combine is believed to operate-
Up to this point, there is an almost identical view with respect to this proposal and the section in the old Combines Act which apparently has been repealed. But the Combines Act then went on to say:
The Director shall
(a) on application made under section 7-
And section 7 is the section I just read. So, obviously there is an injunction laid on the director to make an inquiry, from which inquiry may or may not stem prosecutions, or at least further proceedings. Therefore, I am inclined to accept the principle here, although I would be much happier if the minister thought there was any merit to it, to include the same provision establishing the bona tides of the people making complaint, that they should file with it a statutory declaration giving some details of the nature of the complaint. If that were added, then this provision, to all intents and purposes, would be on all fours with the section in the old Combines Act. I like the principle. All of us talk too much about people becoming involved in the public life of the country. If the people have anything to be concerned about it is certainly the question of pollution, the effect it has on the air they breathe, and the establishment of standards to make it a better environment. I am not decrying the possibility that the government may take action. It may well take action.
However, it would be an admirable thing to establish a sort of court of last resort to which people could lodge complaints, properly verified, and say to the government, "Here is our statutory declaration which says that a certain industry or device is emitting noxious vapours which are having a serious effect on our health and livelihood." Your Honour will remember a situation which arose near Toronto and which was the subject of a television program. A number of people had reason to believe that a factory in the area was poisoning the atmosphere. All they could do was complain to the federal and provincial authorities; they had no right to do anything on their own.
Assuming there would be some instance when this or some other government would not want to take action, I 24171-35

think it would be a good idea if these six people, lodging a complaint properly verified, could compel the minister to launch an inquiry. To that extent, I see no difference between this proposal and the one in the Combines Investigation Act which this government took away from the people. Like the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), I am not too happy with the clause in its present form. I should like to see it changed to have additional safeguards, but the principle is one which I can support. speechtext:
I should like to remind the House that we are considering two amendments which, almost identical in form, nevertheless deal with different parts of the bill. Generally speaking, they focus attention on the right of citizens to take action as a group under the act. I think I can say that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) is not completely wedded to the text of his amendment. There is no particular magic in the use of the number six; it could as easily be five but six happens to be the number of persons required to lodge complaints under the Combines Investigation Act.
Motion No. 11 deals with that part of the bill which refers to offences under the act and clause 33 of the bill is headed "Offences". I refer hon. members to that second amendment to emphasize that, whether its form is correct or not, and whether it is required in each of the places in the bill which the two amendments together suggest, nevertheless it points up a real deficiency in the bill. If I read it correctly, as the bill now stands the only recourse of citizens who may consider themselves aggrieved is to the courts. In other words, if somebody writes to the minister with a complaint he could be told to take it to the courts. This may be very well with some legislation, but in this kind of legislation it is not fair that citizens should be told to lay a charge in court. We are dealing with something very complex here, and it is difficult for the ordinary citizen to determine whether the act is being violated. I think clause 5 of the bill is very appropriate.
As the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) pointed out, this clause provides machinery for the minister to consult with organizations or citizens interested in any aspect of the quality of the ambient air or the control or abatement of air pollution. When they assess the results of the act, and the results of the situation created by various activities within the country, these consulting groups may be operating to a greater or lesser degree. Clause 5 puts the responsibility for this sort of thing on the minister. The effect of the amendment is to reverse the order of things and to give citizens, as of right, in a group of reasonable size the opportunity to take the initiative with the minister and say, "On' the grounds that we have been able to present, we feel there is an unsatisfactory state of affairs in respect of the quality of the ambient air in our neighbourhood and that contaminants which are harmful are going into the envi-

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
ronment." It would give them a channel for their complaint to be investigated by public hearing. This surely is a much more reasonable approach than simply saying, "If you don't like it, take it to court".
It seems to me that the spirit and intent of this legislation is to get people working in co-operation toward a cleaner environment. This objective is not achieved by creating a state of affairs where the only means of correction is through the courts. My understanding of the proposal is to eliminate the need for legal action, particularly if it has to be taken by the citizen. This, I think, is an important consideration for the success of the effort which the minister I think envisages as flowing from the legislation.
There may well be some better way of dealing with the situation than under the exact wording proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I believe the House should recognize that there is a need for a channel of the kind proposed so that a group of citizens may lay a complaint and know that the matter will be looked into properly. Perhaps there should be some discretionary power in the bill for the minister or a responsible person to assess whether there is a preliminary base for a full-scale investigation. However, there should be this channel through which people can move when they feel that the quality of the surrounding air is such that it constitutes a grievance for them.
They should not move through this channel frivolously, and some basis should be established for making sure that complaints are reasonable, particularly if the law requires that substantial public funds be spent in conducting public inquiries. There should be that basis for an inquiry which is essentially designed to ascertain the facts and to say whether there is or is not a situation in a particular area which warrants correcting. I hope the minister and the House will recognize that there is this need.
In British Columbia a good deal of hostility developed over the question of whether an industrial undertaking should go forward in one area on the coast, which happened to be in my constituency, because people felt that the sort of hearings provided under the pollution control legislation of the province did not give them an opportunity adequately to put forward the points of view and the facts as they saw them before the pollution control board rendered its decision. I am sure the minister will agree that we do not want that kind of "snarly" situation to arise in connection with the administration of this legislation and that it would be much better to provide a fairly accessible vehicle for the hearing of complaints so that people could have an opportunity to present the facts as they see them about a situation.
The matter could be examined by scientific experts and the pros and cons aired at a public hearing. There could be an increase in public knowledge and understanding and a determination, clear enough for all to see, regarding whether a certain industrial activity-shall we say a pulp mill on one side of the Ottawa River or an industri-

al plant in any other part of the country-was meeting the standards laid down. It could be determined whether there was deterioration of the atmosphere and whether corrective action needed to be taken.
One danger, as I see it, of our passing this kind of law and of setting up a ministry of the environment is that citizens may be inclined to say, "This has all been fixed. They passed a law in Ottawa and from now on the air will be beautiful." If things do not happen quickly, a feeling of resentment and frustration will build up and people will say, "Nothing has happened." The law itself may begin to fall into disrepute and disrespect in the eyes of citizens. I think it is important for us to provide some kind of proper channel, which does not now exist in the bill, whereby people can to their reasonable satisfaction lay complaints on the table, as it were, have them dealt with properly by a body, tribunal or hearing officer and thereby feel that the situation has been assessed fairly and a determination has been made on the basis of facts they have laid before the tribunal and of further facts elicited from people properly qualified to determine whether there are proper grounds for complaint and whether the act has been violated.
That is the purpose behind these two amendments. I hope no one in the House will quibble over whether the phrasing of the motion in question is exactly as it should be to meet the situation, because I am certain that if the minister would recognize the need and suggest a modification of the existing provision that would more properly in his view meet the situation, the hon. member for Kootenay West would sympathetically listen to his suggestion. We could then quickly work out something which would obtain the unanimous approval of the House.
The minister has not yet spoken on this matter. He may rise and say that these two motions deal adequately with the situation that has been drawn to the attention of the House. If he does, we will be happy and I am sure we can pass these motions without further debate. On the other hand, if the minister feels they can be improved upon I am certain the hon. member for Kootenay West will be willing to listen to and possibly agree on alternative proposals or modifications so long as the need is met for a channel through which citizens can make their complaints known. Once they have established that there are reasonable grounds for complaint, they ought to know that there will be a hearing where a determination will be made on the facts and reasonable action taken without their going through the difficult process of laying formal charges in court, which otherwise would be their sole recourse for correcting an unsatisfactory situation.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the purpose of the motion is to require the government to shoulder its responsibilities under clause 5(2) of the legislation. This is more or less the point we have been hammering at all afternoon. The motion provides that if the government does not shoulder its responsibilities and set up inquiries when inquiries are needed, six citizens can force it to do so. This is a clear indication to the public to take part in the process of
June 21, 1971

government. It is something that is now being seriously discussed in Canadian and American circles, this is, the right of citizens to take action to protect the environment and not have to wait for the government, the courts or anyone else to do so. For that reason I think this is a good amendment and deserves acceptance.
The public is pretty well excluded from putting pressure on the government, particularly since it has been clearly indicated that we will not get acceptance of amendments Nos. 3 and 5 which puts the onus on the government to do certain things. It is a matter of contention whether the citizen's right to move into the environmental field and force the government to take action is effective. There is some feeling that litigation in the courts is expensive for an individual or group of individuals unless there is backing at the national level. There is a feeling that in a number of cases such a provision which is being written into statutes concerning the environment may be ineffective. Under this amendment any six citizens would have the right to initiate an inquiry if they felt their environment was being adversely affected.
I have one hesitation in this respect. It has already been expressed and was implied in the question of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman). How many of these so-called inquiries could the government stand? Could a group of 25 citizens get together one evening and decide to hit the government with four inquiries, with each group of six people signing a separate petition?
Protection was provided under the old section of the combines legislation which was referred to by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). If citizens raised a complaint and it was verified by statutory declaration, the director was required to proceed with an investigation provided he had reason to believe that the facts stated were correct and an inquiry was warranted. The protection the government had was that six people could not force an inquiry of their own volition, but they could very easily initiate the procedure. I know that the director of the combines investigation branch considers it his duty to conduct an inquiry into every valid and legitimate complaint that is raised.
Perhaps this amendment could have been worded a little better to give some protection to the government. But if the privilege that is given to citizens is abused, it is not very difficult for us to amend the statute. We have that protection and we can act on it quickly. In fact, by the time these inquiries start we can bring in amendments if there is serious abuse.
The principle of the amendment is one that we should accept. On balance, even if there are not enough safeguards written into it, it ought to be accepted. If Parliament finds that there are abuses, we can very quickly amend the legislation. There is very little evidence of

Mr. Speaker, it appears to me the government ought to welcome the amendments suggested in motions Nos. 6 and 11. One of the few advantages of the Combines Investigation Act is the extent to which attention is called by experts and others to various offences which take place. Where experts are involved, people who are vitally interested in certain specific areas bring to the attention of the director responsible for the administration of the act information which allows him to proceed with investigations which often result in changes which are of great advantage to the public. In the main, this is done by people who are experts in particular fields.
I was interested in an article which appeared today in the Globe and Mail. It was written by David Spurgeon, under the heading, "Danger to the environment in a nuclear power plant". He writes:
The agenda of the Canadian Nuclear Association's annual international conference, which begins today in Montreal, is curiously devoid of the kind of issue that currently is rocking the foundations of the nuclear power industry in the United States.
Concern for the environment there has recently prompted a group of prominent scientists to sue the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission. Concern about the safety of nuclear power plants lias prompted two famous opponents of the A EC, Dr. John W. Gofman and Dr. Arthur R. Tamplin, to publish a new book called "Poisoned Power, The Case Against Nuclear Electric Plants"-a hard hitting attack on some of the assumptions underlying the development of nuclear power aimed at citizens' groups.
Senator Mike Gravel of Alaska has declared his strong support for the suit announced by the Scientists' Institute for Public Information, an organization of 35 distinguished U.S. scientists whose purpose is to provide ordinary citizens with information about scientific aspects of public policy, headed by anthropologist Margaret Mead.
I am bound to say that in my judgment an agency of this kind would be most helpful to the minister if he is
[Mr. Knowles (Norfolk-Haldimand) .1
really interested in ending pollution. In the past, governments have been content to wait until a problem was obviously on their doorstep. A case in point is the Ottawa River. For years ministers have been saying they intend to clean it up. Finally it was left to the two provinces directly concerned to decide that something should be done. I understand there is now to be a conference. Well, had they wanted to delay any longer I suppose they could have waited until all the municipalities along the river had become involved.
If the minister intends to follow the practices of the past, no doubt the government will from time to time find cases which warrant investigation and occasionally something will be done when it becomes absolutely necessary. But such an approach is far from adequate today and in confirmation we need only consider the concern expressed in the United States as to the effects of nuclear emissions in the air and the danger these may cause.
The average citizen does not know whether or not many of the pollutants now in the air are dangerous. It is said that around some plants the emissions are so strong that they would take the paint off a car. But no one has yet dropped dead walking through a parking lot so I suppose citizens generally will not become much concerned until conditions are so bad that action cannot be avoided. Usually, though, before such a point is reached a private individual, usually a doctor or a scientist, finds some means of calling attention to the danger. I have found such people more than willing to become involved in this type of business; they are willing to provide the scientific background and pinpoint the danger before it becomes apparent to the average citizen. Services of this kind make an excellent contribution to the effectiveness of a bill such as the one before us. This would be especially so if machinery were established along the lines of that contemplated in the amendments, enabling the minister to receive and act upon such information.
If, on the other hand, the government decides to reserve all the decisions in this field to itself, I believe the result will be decisions which are politically motivated. No doubt some investigations will be carried out, but the legislation will get off to a slow start. I think it would be a very foolish government which would ignore suggestions put before it by people who were experts in particular areas.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deach-man) asked a question which emphasized the ultra-conservative attitude prevalent among members of the government party when he wondered what would happen should a large number of these people bring cases before a commission of inquiry. It would cost a lot of money, he suggested, a great many people would be occupied on these cases and there would be a formidable backlog of inquiries. I do not think any Member of Parliament who receives a normal amount of mail fails to have called to his attention at least once or twice a week cases concerning the destruction of our environment which would justify inquiry. I continually receive letters from constituents who say that municipal sewage is overflowing, that raw sewage is flowing into the Ottawa River via Lake Timiskaming, and so on. Seldom a week goes by in
June 21, 1971

which people do not write to tell me that one of the lumber companies', one of the pulp companies or a local flakeboard operation is polluting rivers or lakes.
I noticed an editorial in my local paper the other day which indicated that the pollution of Lake Timiskaming was caused mostly by clay. We live in the clay belt and cannot control run-off or clay wash into Lake Timiskaming, which eventually runs down to the Ottawa Eiver, a body of water that the federal government is going to pay millions of dollars to make fresh once again. I am sure each member receives complaints about pollution. Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra does not pass them on for the simple reason that too much trouble would be caused the government in investigating them. He asked what would happen if a large number of people reported complaints and said we would have so many courts of inquiry that we could not handle them.
The point I am trying to make is that in my riding about 15 different points of information a month in regard to pollution come to my notice. I am sure there would be inquiries into them if only we had someone to whom to refer them. I would guess that 50 per cent of these complaints would be substantiated and the pollutants concerned found detrimental to the environment and ordered to be eliminated. Not only do I think that is true, but I am sure the minister does too, otherwise he would not introduce this kind of legislation. The House has passed at least two other pieces of legislation dealing with pollution, and I am sure the minister would not have accepted the responsibility of Minister of the Environment had cases of the sort I have cited not been substantiated.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra stated that if six people made a good case, a commission of inquiry would have to be established. That may well be true. But that in itself should in no way be an objection to such a proposal. If that is the case, it means that things are a lot worse than we think they are and if necessary we should have 1,000 or 2,000 such inquiries. Someone should be in a position to say that a given complaint warrants an investigation or full-scale inquiry. Other cases could be referred to a particular department for attention. A commission of inquiry would not necessarily have to be established in assessing what action to take. The department will develop expertise in such matters and will be able to examine complaints itself.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) who administers the Combines Investigation Act would be first to admit that if individuals lost their right to complain it would often be very difficult to bring problems to the attention of the government. In this particular case a complaint would have to be endorsed by six individuals, not one. That is why I feel the amendment is reasonable. The minister can inform us whether his department has sufficient funds to set up such inquiries and he can also say whether he feels it necessary to have a full-scale commission of inquiry in such cases. Perhaps he can suggest a more simplified way of dealing with complaints that are not possible of easy solution.
Clean Air Act
We do not suggest that the six complainants receive a share of any fine that is imposed, as is often the case when offences are committed of a criminal nature. I believe the Customs Act provides for a person who makes a charge which is proved to receive a kickback or portion of the fine imposed. Neither are we suggesting that people be hired to make reports. I suggest the greatest indication of the need of this amendment is the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra that the only reason the government will oppose the amendment is that there will be so many inquiries.
At the present time Ontario is rapidly developing sources of nuclear power, yet even the experts who attended the recent international conference on nuclear power are not considering pollution of the environment, even though they are discussing breeder plants which produce plutonium which itself presents a great danger to the environment. The reason this subject is not being discussed is that all the government experts in this field are members of the nuclear colony. Their employment at universities or in the nuclear field in Canada gives them a living. I suggest that some of the research done by United States universities in this field should be brought to the attention of the minister. If the minister does not see any merit in a well-documented complaint that is made by six citizens of the calibre I expect to be involved in making such complaint, then I would suggest he is not really interested in ambient air quality or in doing anything about controlling air pollution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, amendment No. 7 is a most important amendment which
we are offering to the bill. For a number of months we have been urging the federal government to set up national standards so far as air pollutants are concerned. We fought a similar fight last year in respect of the Canada Water Act; we were interested in having national standards which would apply from one end of Canada to the other.
We are getting down to the same thing in respect of this bill. I should like hon. members to turn to clause 7. I am convinced a large number of members really do not understand what is in this clause. It is headed "National emission standards and guidelines". Canadians generally feel we are about to establish national standards for emissions from industry throughout the country. What are really to be set up under the bill are emission standards for only a handful of pollutants.
These are emissions which constitute a significant danger to the health of persons. Never in my life have I seen a weaker clause than this one. What does it mean? I shall touch on the problem very generally. I do not have very much time now, and I should 1 ke hon. members to study the clause over the supper hour. The phrase used is "a significant danger to the health of persons". This means we cannot do anything about the hydrogen sulphide emissions which come from the Eddy plant across the river in Hull and produce odours which permeate our air. We are not setting up emission standards to control hydrogen sulphide, for the simple reason that medical authorities say hydrogen sulphide has not shown indications of being a pollutant which is injurious to the health of people. So the residents of Ottawa and Hull will have to put up with this type of pollutant because it is not covered by the clause. This is utter nonsense.
This clause does not cover any pollutant which might cause damage to a person's house or motor car. It does not cover any damage which might be done to wildlife or vegetation. During the committee hearings when witnesses were being questioned we learned that only a
Clean Air Act
handful of the standards set will be national in scope, dealing with things such as mercury. This is a step forward. It involves mercury and things of that nature because they are a significant danger to the health of persons. The amendment which we have brought in and which we are asking the minister and the government to consider I again draw to the attention of members of the House. The amendment reads in part:
The Governor in Council shall prescribe national emission standards establishing the quantities, if any, and concentrations in which any air contaminant may not be emitted into the ambient air from sources of any class, whether stationary or mobile, when such emissions shall constitute a danger to the health of persons or cause an appreciable damage to property or to the quality of the environment.
Then the amendment goes on to touch the international field which is very similar to the legislation proposed in the bill.
Air pollution is one of the major problems facing Canadians today. We could have several emissions coming from a smokestack; we could have particles of sawdust and soot. All these things could not be touched under this legislation although they could interfere in a host of ways with the quality of life we are supposed to be able to enjoy while living in areas surrounding industrial plants. If the legislation should go through as it is now offered to the House, we will be faced with all kinds of problems. I suggest to the minister that during the supper hour he and his staff get together and change the wording of the clause in such a way that it will provide some protection in respect of the points I have in mind and on which I should like to expand when we reassemble at eight o'clock.
I return to the point about a significant danger to the health of persons. What does this mean? There is no interpretation clause in the legislation. Does it mean one must be just a little ill from pollutants?
