speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned at six o'clock we were discussing the amendment which I had proposed to clause 7. I think I should spnd just a moment or two reviewing it. The amendment we are offering would expand the clause to include pollutants which might affect aesthetic values and which, for example, could effect buildings, wildlife, etc. Before we adjourned I was pointing out that this is the key part of the bill. I cannot emphasize this too much. Here in Canada, in 1971, we are bringing in what we call a clean air act and under it we are going to set standards.
The general feeling of Canadians is that a number of national standards will be set respecting control of air pollution and the point I was making is that this just is not so. This is not what the legislation is all about and that is why we are complaining. We think that considerations other than that of a significant danger to health must be taken into account.
We had a very lengthy debate on this clause in the committee. Various witnesses gave their opinions. The minister gave a fairly plausible reason why we should not change the clause. I shall read the clause because I think hon. members should thoroughly understand what they will be voting on. Clause 7, which will become law unless we change it, reads as follows:
Where the emission into the ambient air of an air contaminant in the quantities and concentrations in which it is consumed or produced in the operation of stationary sources of a particular class or classes specified by the Governor in Council would-
And these are the key words
(a) constitute a significant danger to the health of persons ... the Governor in Council may prescribe national emission standards establishing the maximum quantities, if any, and concentrations of such air contaminant that may be emitted into the ambient air by stationary sources of such class or classes.
As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, this provision will not stop any pulp mill in the country fouling the air of a district such as Ottawa or any other part of the country. I drew the attention of hon. members to the odour of hydrogen sulphide which medical people tell us is not a significant danger to health. This means that we can do nothing about it under the clean air act. If it is not a danger to health, I think one of the most offensive things that can happen to a community is to be exposed to this rotten egg odour. This is the sort of thing we should be legislating against but it will not be covered by the act. Presumably, if a company wanted to increase the hydrogen sulphide emission from their stacks nothing could be done about it. I see nothing in this act to deal with the problem. There are many such problems all over the country which will not be touched by the act.
The government intends to set national standards for mercury and fluoride, but the question our party asks is why such standards cannot be set for all the pollutants
emitted by industry. We hope this will come about. One type of emission from a smokestack may cause a skin rash, but in the bill there is no definition in respect of "a significant danger to health". Soot and other particles can be emitted, but are they not a significant danger to health? Where do we draw the line? The people of Canada will get little assistance from this clause; that is why we are urging the minister to make changes along the lines suggested in my amendment. Health, of course, is of primary importance but we think the whole problem should be considered in the following terms:
-when such emissions shall constitute a danger to the health of persons or cause an appreciable damage to property or to the quality of the environment.
Any emissions which damage property, wildlife or vegetation should be legislated against. They cost the taxpayer money and naturally are of concern. Every Canadian, Mr. Speaker, has the right to breathe clean air and live in a decent environment, the right to enjoy some of the aesthetic advantages of his surroundings. We should be able to prevent industry creating smog to the point where it is impossible to see across a valley. Surely this is part of our duty as legislators.
We must not allow these things to happen because of weak legislation. We should be in a position to take a strong line with industry. It would not take place in a week or ten days, but over a period of time we must be able to control industry to the point where we can say, "The air of Canada belongs to Canadians. They have a right to good, clean air from one end of the country to the other, and that is what we are aiming for."
I know that a number of hon. members wish to speak to the amendment, Mr. Speaker, so I shall say no more except to point out that this provision is the key to the bill. It is the weakest clause in the bill. It will not give Canada national standards as far as air contaminants are concerned, and this is what we are after. We put up a fight for national standards under the Canada Water Act, and did not get them. It now looks as though we shall not get them under the clean air act. I suggest that the government has drafted weak legislation and urge it to reconsider the bill before it is too late.

subtopic: CLEAN AIR ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE RELATING TO AMBIENT AIR QUALITY AND CONTROL OF POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) when he spoke on amendment No. 7 and suggested that clause 7 be amended as follows:
-by deleting lines 27 to 35 inclusive at page 6 and lines 1 to 13 inclusive at page 7 and substituting the following therefor:
"7. (1) The Governor in Council shall prescribe national emission standards establishing the quantities, if any, and concentrations in which any air contaminant may not be emitted into the ambient air from sources of any class, whether stationary or mobile, when such emissions shall constitute a danger to the health of persons or cause an appreciable damage to property or to the quality of the environment.
(2) In no instance shall these standards prescribed violate a term or terms of any international obligation entered into by the government of Canada relating to the control or abatement of air pollution in regions adjacent to any international boundary or throughout the world."

June 21, 1971

As the mover of the amendment has stated, this is an important clause. It was thoroughly discussed and debated when the bill was before committee. We in the official opposition expressed our concern about it. We have an amendment which asks for a definition of the expressions:
"endangers the health, safety or welfare of persons", "interferes with normal enjoyment of life", "endangers the health of animal life", "causes damage to plant life", and "constitutes a significant danger to the health of persons"-*
The terminology concerns us. However, Mr. Speaker, like so many of the amendments which come from that section of the House, this one is desirable but in our opinion is not practical at the present time. I say that because in my view the key words in this amendment are ''stationary or mobile". I point out, Sir, that when we debated motions 1 and 2 this afternoon we objected to the inclusion of "mobile" because we felt that the automobile industry and the mode of transportation which has been adopted for the sake of convenience by many Canadians would become prematurely obsolete if that type of amendment were permitted.
We understand that it is now the law in most provinces that emission systems installed in cars in or after 1970 must be such as to control toxic emissions from exhausts. These systems are being installed at the time of manufacture and are to minimize pollution from automobile exhaust systems. There is already co-operation on this question between provincial governments and the automobile industry. The United States is also concerned about the pollution of its air. Many of our automobiles are manufactured in the United States and since companies in Canada are subsidiaries of large United States entreprises we can expect continued co-operation in this area. Within the next five years, I believe, the obsolescence of automobiles will create a difference in the volume of exhaust pollution in our air because cars which have been coming on the market since 1970 are equipped with an emission control system.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we in the official opposition cannot support the amendment as proposed. It would create considerable difficulty for those who use automobiles, and for our airlines. Our airlines are working on the problem of emission but have not yet been able to conquer it completely. Concern over this matter was expressed to the committee in many different ways. May I put on record, as an example, the views of the Petroleum Association for Conservation of the Environment as expressed by J. D. Lovering. Among other things, he said:
The terms "air quality objectives", "national emission guidelines" and "national emission standards" are confusing. Under section 2 only "air quality objectives" are defined. We suggest that "national emission guidelines" and "national emission standards" are also given definitions under section 2.
The provision for "air quality objectives" on a national basis is to be commended. Nevertheless, the intention regarding national emission standards needs to be clarified. If emission standards are to be based on an approach consistent with the "air quality objectives" and on actual measurements of ambient air quality, then this would seem rational. If, however, the intention is to adopt national emission standards without reference 24-171-36
Clean Air Act
to the existing variable air quality for different regions of Canada, then such standards would seem most impractical.
That, in part, expresses the concern of the Petroleum Association for Conservation of the Environment in Canada. The problem will be dealt with if the minister, representing the federal government, in co-operation with industry works out within as brief a period as possible a program for cutting down pollution. As we all know, pollution is injurious to the health of Canadians, and since the air surrounding the globe knows no international boundaries it is also injurious to the health of citizens in all parts of the world.
Before I resume my seat I should like to make one other point dealing with emissions from a mobile source. Automobiles, for example, would be affected if this motion were passed and we therefore question whether we have authority to deal with this matter now inasmuch as the control of automobiles is vested in the provincial governments. They have the right to build highways and to licence automobiles, and it is a licence and not a right. Since this matter, to my knowledge, has not been worked out by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) and the provinces, I doubt whether this type of amendment would be acceptable. For these reasons we in the official opposition cannot support the motion.

speechtext:
May I now turn to suggestion that our dealing with this matter would not be constitutional. I have some experience in constitutional matters and have often found that the Constitution is trotted out as an excuse when someone does not want to deal with a subject. I assure the House that as far as I can make out-and I speak on the basis of previous experience- the right of Parliament to enact legislation dealing with pollution of the air by prohibition and by the setting of national standards is abundantly clear. We should not allow this suggestion to deter us from doing that which we believe is necessary.
I mentioned earlier in the debate that the key to this legislation is adequate enforcement. Reams of legislation have been passed on this type of subject. As you know, Mr. Speaker, practically the whole law of public nuisance has been directed to this particular field. Yet the weakness of all efforts in the past has resided in the lack of adequate enforcement. I think the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) has put his finger on the

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
major weakness in the bill. Clause 7 is the core of the bill since it deals with the setting of national standards in respect of emission. What do we find in that clause? We find in it a phrase through which a lawyer acting for a pollutant company will be able to win his case without any difficulty. What is the phrase? For the purposes of this debate I will not go into clause 7(l)(b), but clause 7(l)(a) provides:
-constitute a significant danger to the health of persons-
As the hon. member for Kootenay West said, by using such weak, ambiguous phrases as that you rob the bill of its effectiveness. A pollutant company will not have trouble in getting a medical expert to say, "We are not in a position to say that this type of pollution of the air constitutes a significant danger to health. It might or it might not. In any event, we do not know what 'significant' means and we do not know what sort of danger to health you are talking about." I can just imagine the cases in which those who pollute the air will escape the provisions of the bill because of the weakness of those words. Clearly, they need to be strengthened in accordance with the proposal of the hon. member for Kootenay West. All sorts of polluting substances may or may not constitute a substantial or significant danger to health.
I told the House earlier that pollution in my constituency, a very attractive residential area, has been found to be a most serious problem by a private group known as Forward 9 Citizens' Association. It is a non-partisan association which has set up a task force on pollution and has studied the problem in an area that I advisedly call a very attractive residential area. What have they found? I will not go through all their findings; I mentioned them earlier. In part, however, they found that an incinerator operated by the metropolitan Toronto works department is causing local problems. They say:
Odours, fly ash, and black smoke are regularly emitted from its three stacks. Garbage is not separated into different kinds and no attempt is made to remove the specific types of garbage that create troublesome emissions when they are burned. Only one of the three stacks has even a partially effective precipitator. The plant is frequently used to burn many more tons a day than it was designed to handle (even though this practice is illegal!)
Most of the fly ash reaching us here in ward 9-
The area to which they are referring is part of my constituency.
-consists of small particles, which leave a coating of soot on exposed surfaces. Closer to the incinerator, in residential areas of wards 7 and 8, the ash that falls is much denser and larger (with flakes sometimes the size of quarters) and gives rise to serious problems: cars change colour overnight, ash has to be shovelled off porches, windows have to be kept closed, exterior paintwork is ruined (and fresh paint immediately spoiled), and washing hung out to dry can be made dirty within an hour or two.
They invite the people who dump this ash to come and see it for themselves. It is a great problem. A similar problem arises from the sewage plant at Ashbridge's Bay.
They say there are four stacks that regularly emit smoke in large amounts. They further say:
Foul and highly offensive smells blow from the aeration tanks and sludge lagoons at the plant to residential areas to the north
and east.
Raw sewage goes through the plant into the lake.
I suppose that is a matter for the water control legislation.
AH three kinds of pollution call for immediate attention and control.
The least serious problem is probably the smoke coming from the stacks, which is caused by the burning of dried sludge.
The obnoxious odours from the aeration tanks are a far more immediate hazard. At times the smells reach nauseating levels and afflict thousands of people in nearby residential areas. Methods are being tried to counteract the odour by spraying a deodorant into the air, but residents know that this method doesn't work.
When it rains in Toronto, the quality of the effluent from the plant decreases as the rainfall increases. This is because the sewage system consists largely of combined sewers, handling both storm and sanitary sewage, (and is) unable to handle the load and raw sewage flows into the lake. A program of separating the two systems is under way but is not scheduled for completion until 1990. Meanwhile, the lake becomes more and more polluted. Why should we wait 20 years?
The point I want to draw to the attention of the minister is that although these conditions are objectionable and destroy the quality of life of people living in the area-this problem is not unique; I speak from experience in my constituency and am familiar with it-they are duplicated in many parts of Canada. None of this can be shown to be a substantial danger to health. Because it is only a danger to the amenity and the quality of life, it will escape unscathed. People who live in this excellent residential area have to put up with these odours. They should not have to put up with them if we mean what we say about maintaining clean air.
I wish to draw another subject to the attention of the minister although it may be a little off the point. The people in my constituency were extremely encouraged by the statement the minister made on march 16 to the Special Committee on Environmental Pollution. The minister promised the following:
The federal government likely will conduct research into ways of disposing of solid wastes without burning them. .. Knowledge from such studies will be of great help to cities such as Toronto which must dispose of tons of garbage every day.
If this bill is not tightened up, much of what we are talking about with regard to disposal of garbage-and there is some concern whether it constitutes a substantial hazard to health-will be found to be impossible. The minister went on to say:
Financial assistance to municipalities to help them deal with their garbage problem also may be provided by the federal government at a later date-
I say to the minister, "More power to you." If he goes ahead with plans of that sort he will contribute a great deal to the future of this country, particularly the future of the area I represent. In conclusion I say that the

June 21, 1971

amendment proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, is essential to the adequate enforcement of this act. Without it, it will be easy for powerful interests which are guilty of polluting the atmosphere of our country to escape under legalistic excuses because the bill is so inadequately drawn that it does not prohibit their continuing to pollute.

Mr. Speaker, I hear one of my good friends across the way faintly groaning. I suppose all one can do at this stage of the session is to speak or groan faintly. Nevertheless, I would like to do a little of one or both for a few minutes.
As already pointed out, the subject matter of this amendment is central to whether the bill will be adequate and sound, a piece of legislation that will meet the challenges that the Canadian people feel should be met in this area. Now that the bill is back in this chamber at the report stage, it has gone full circle. I do not know whether we have made any progress, because what we are discussing in this amendment was the central theme in the second reading debate and what intervened in committee did not result in any change in this clause. However, I feel justified in coming back to it again because it is a very crucial question.
I suggest in my speech on second reading that the stuff and substance of this bill, in particular the amendment we are considering, are the building blocks of a new Constitution for Canada. As indicated by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), the matter was pursued in committee. Some of the questioning that took place in committee with regard to clause 7 was closely tied in with the whole question of establishment of national standards, not only as to whether this was desirable but constitutional.
One of the witnesses who appeared before our committee was a representative of the Department of Justice. Questions were directed to him. I wish to refer briefly to page 22 of report No. 2 of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, where Mr. Gibson was answering questions. One of the questions asked what had been done by way of research into the constitutional foundation of the bill. Mr. Gibson replied:
I understand the questions related to the degree of constitutional research that was done in the stages of preparation of this bill. In answering that question I can only indicate what was done within the Department of Justice and what was made available to me, as an officer of the Department of Justice, by other departments.
There was very extensive review of the proposals which gave rise to this bill within the Department of Justice from a constitutional viewpoint. I do not know how much further I can go other than to simply say that the matter was considered within the department at all levels up to and including both the level of the deputy minister and the minister himself. There was no outside advice retained by the Department of Justice to my knowledge and I think my knowledge is complete. I am not
Clean Air Act
aware of any outside legal advice which was received by the Department of National Health and Welfare at the early stages or by the Department of Fisheries and Forestry.
In response to a question concerning federal responsibility for air, Mr. Gibson said:
I have great difficulty in dealing with air in abstract.
A little later he said:
I do not look upon air per se as being a subject of jurisdiction either federal or provincial. Certainly it is not listed in section 91 of the BNA Act nor in section 92. Unless you somehow extrapolate from the listings in those sections-and I have grave difficulty doing that directly in relation to air-no, I would not be prepared to say that air is in essence a subject of jurisdiction either of the federal Parliament or the provincial legislatures.
So there you have it. Mr. Gibson was saying, as an officer of the Department of Justice, that the question of air is one for which the Constitution does not provide. I was interested in the contribution to the debate on the constitutional aspect made by my hon. friend from Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). He stated a side of the case which was largely ignored in committee, namely, the degree of jurisd ction under the criminal law. It is obvious the government has operated within the traditional hidebound framework of the British North America Act. We discussed this question in committee. The Minister of Fisheries, now Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) again emphasized the propriety of federal jurisdiction in matters concerning health and in relation to international dealings, while completely ignoring the broader context in which we should be considering this subject.
The bill with which we are dealing has been before the House for some time. 1 have made a practice, when meeting Canadians in various parts of the country with various degrees of knowledge to ask what they thought we should be doing. In private conversation at a conference in Toronto, where 1 had an opportunity to meet people from many parts of Canada, this was the theme: Do you feel that in light of the facts before us, despite our incomplete knowlege, this situation should be regarded as a national and international question, one which should be dealt with as a subject of national jurisdiction? Is this necessary for the future of our people? Almost invariably the answer I received was: Yes, this is the approach we should be taking; there must be national standards if we are to get anywhere.
Here we are today at the report stage of the bill-just about where we were when we started, as far as practical issues are concerned. Those who are in a position to take the lead seem to be ignoring the issue completely. Recently a conference was held in Victoria, the capital city of my province. Was this question on the agenda? Do not hon. members agree that this is one of the most practical and urgent matters which should have been discussed at that conference? Could we not have said to the Premiers gathered there: In a developing international crisis of which we are part, should we be content with the traditional approaches to the interpretation of the Constitution? Are you not prepared to give the federal Parliament authority to move in and deal with this matter in a way which is adequate to the circumstances?
24171-36j

June 21, 1971
Clean Air Act
But no, we took the approach of dealing with the Constitution as though it were something abstract, up in the clouds, something which ordinary citizens need not be concerned about. It is only a token gesture under which Members of Parliament are allowed to discuss the Constitution and listen to the views of citizens. As a little sop to the existence of Parliament, the co-chairmen of the constitutional committee were allowed to go to Victoria and sit at the fringe of the conference. Admittedly, some of the issues dealt with there are important, it is well we should spend time discussing the relationship of groups within our society. But unless we in this Parliament and in this country are prepared to come to grips with any constitutional obstruction which may exist to a solution of this question, we might as well forget about worrying which language group will survive and in what circumstances.
I say the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was derelict in his duty in not having placed a topic like this in the forefront of the subjects to be discussed at that conference. This is why an attempt is made now to brush these amendments aside as though they are minor matters which are thrown in for debate at the end of a parliamentary session. This is the challenge which the Minister of the Environment has been refusing to face, despite his fine speeches. I submit in all seriousness that when members opposite vote on the amendment they should consider it in this context and realize its importance to the future well-being of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, this is another important amendment. We are suggesting to the government that once the clean air bill has passed the House some kind of timetable should be established for industry to bring its plants into line with the standards and objectives that are set. When this matter was debated during the committee stage there was some objection to the amendment. Some hon. members felt it would be unfair to some industry if it did not have, say, more than a five-year period in which to clean up its pollution. As a result, this amendment seeks to add a third subclause giving the minister the right, in cases where the circumstances warrant, to extend the period of five years, subject to an annual review by the minister. This takes care of the objections of those who feel that an industry which had not eliminated its pollution might have to close down after a five-year period.
Let not the Canadian public kid itself, Mr. Speaker: Canada is in trouble as far as its environment is concerned. In fact, the whole world is in trouble as a result of emissions into the air and pollution of the water, whether from DDT, mercury or just plain sewage. The question is: When are we going to start drawing the line and setting timetables to clean up this pollution?
This afternoon the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) told the House that mobile sources did not have to be brought under the act because there are all kinds of regulations on the statute books of Canada to take care of them. I agree with the minister 100 per cent; we have had pollution regulations in dozens and dozens of statutes. But the trouble is that they have never been enforced.
A year ago I had a survey carried out on a number of pieces of legislation in order to ascertain whether pollution regulations in Canada were being enforced. Mention was made this afternoon of mining. In the seven years previous to last year not one case of mining pollution was taken to the courts or reported. Dozens and dozens of infractions occur all over Canada, especially in the north, where we have jurisdiction, but there are no prosecutions. This is why we are worried. In our national parks, in some instances raw sewage is getting into the rivers and streams; yet only one case in the whole of Canada, namely in Banff national park, which warranted a $5 fine, was reported.
Since there are regulations on the books which the government has not been enforcing, we prefer to bring them all under the umbrella of the minister. We think he is the one to handle the problem. He should take pride in the fact that we have confidence both in him and his department to do the job. As I say, this loose enforcement of sxisting regulations gives us cause for concern. We have had enough of the pollution that is taking place. Our

June 21, 1971

rivers and lakes have been turned into sewers. In many sections of the country the air is unfit to breathe. A host of medical problems have arisen due to pollution of the air. The provincial legislatures are afraid to tackle the pollution problem because industry is holding the whip over them and over this Parliament. The government is afraid to move, just as it is afraid to move on some of the taxation measures before the House. This is why we are suggesting a timetable be set in order to let industry know they have so long to clean up the mess. We are giving them all kinds of incentives now, and their antipollution equipment can be written off at our expense in two years.
I recently received an excellent report dealing with pulp mills in Quebec. Hon. members would be frightened if they realized the pollution that is taking place in that province. The minister himself knows it will take years and years to clean up this pollution, especially since there are so many old plants still in operation. Although we have to help industry in some ways to fight pollution, we must at the same time be tough and let industry know that this country belongs to Canadians who have a right to clean air and to clean water.
Although we are not trying to put industry out of business, it has so far avoided dealing with a host of pollution problems. This is why we must set a timetable, publish regulations and insist upon their being carried out. After all, we are here to govern, to tackle problems in Canada and to do this we must make changes to the legislation currently before the House. I appreciate the difficulties industry is facing. We are as much to blame for pollution as industry, because we have let industry continue to pour pollutants into the air and into the water.
But the time has come when the Canadian people must cry halt. The Canadian people cannot go on indefinitely allowing pollutants to be poured into the air and water and to expect this old earth and all the food chain systems in it to survive. In many instances almost irreparable damage has been done. Therefore, I suggest that the minister accept this amendment and include a timetable in the legislation.

subtopic: CLEAN AIR ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE RELATING TO AMBIENT AIR QUALITY AND CONTROL OF POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we intend to support this amendment. I do not think it would have been possible to support it had the hon. member not included subclause 3. Established industries, with large payrolls, that have been in operation for many years in many cases cannot meet the problem of pollution in an immediate way within a period of five years. They may be capable of reducing but certainly not of totally eliminating pollutants.
However, it does seem desirable that a timetable of some sort be inserted in the bill. Otherwise, in many other operations of this legislation the government may or may not move. It may not take action, depending on how it interprets the act or the situation. I believe a general timetable for meeting emission standards within
Clean Air Act
industry is reasonable. If we do not have such a timetable we may never reach the goal toward which this bill is aimed.
It would have been impossible to say that all emission standards must be met by all industry in Canada within a period of five years. That would be highly desirable but in many cases most difficult. There are cases where there must be a reasonable reduction to a point where the government is satisfied real efforts are being made. While there is legislation in existence in the province of Ontario, prosecutions are not undertaken if an industry can prove it is really moving on the problem, is working toward a goal and that it will eventually conquer its pollution problems.
The hon. member has written into this amendment provision for the minister to consider special cases and extend the period within which an industry must meet air standards. Furthermore, it requires that the decision for extension should receive an annual review. I am in agreement with that. If the matter is brought to the attention of the minister each year, it is then up to him and his department to see that efforts have been made before further extension is granted. Therefore, we support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, this amendment was placed on the order paper by my

Clean Air Act
colleague the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) and it is my pleasure to put it forward on his behalf. I will be very brief.
The purpose of the amendment is in line with many of the other amendments brought forward today by opposition parties, that is, to tighten up the administration of the act. We feel that in many cases the definitions and regulations have been too loosely set out in the bill, with too much leeway within which no real decision can be taken. This applies particularly to the definition of what actually constitutes pollution, specifically air pollution.
The interpretation clause does not make any reference to those parts read out by Your Honour, except in general terms. The amendment is intended to allow the Governor in Council to make regulations to define more specifically and precisely fundamental expressions in the interpretation section. This is about all I need say. We feel the act will be better if these definitions are included and the somewhat vague terms expressed in more specific language.

subtopic: CLEAN AIR ACT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a minute or two on this amendment to say why our group will support it. It seems to me the act should include these definitions and I am hopeful the minister will agree. In years to come, if a law suit arises in respect of pollution, clarification in the terms cf the amendment would be essential. There is nothing wrong with such clarification. We should know what "a significant danger to the health of a person" means according to the act. Do you have to be moved on your back on a stretcher, do you have to be on crutches, or what does it mean? What kind of test will doctors carry out to determine whether something is a significant danger to heatlh?
As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) said earlier, these words can mean almost anything. If the matter gets into a court of law one would have a difficult time making a case against a company which was polluting. For this reason the legislation is weak and there should be included in it clarification of these terms. I urge the minister to accept the amendment.

That Bill C-224, an act relating to ambient air quality and to the control of air pollution, be amended by adding the following subclause to clause 39 immediately after line 34 at page 29:
"(3) The Governor in Council, forthwith upon the proclamation of this act, shall cause a study to be made with reference to the feasibility of establishing a fund out of which a person, where no civil remedy is available to him, might recover ex gratia compensation for injury by air pollution to his health, safety or welfare or for interference with his normal enjoyment of his life or property; and the Governor in Council shall cause such study to be made public upon receipt thereof."
Hon. members will remember that at the outset of the report stage on this bill the Chair gave advance notice of its reservation concerning the acceptability of motion No. 12 and stated that hon. members would be given an opportunity to present argument in respect of the acceptability of the motion. I would therefore invite hon. members to present their views on this motion and the Chair will reserve its decision until afterward.

subtopic: CLEAN AIR ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE RELATING TO AMBIENT AIR QUALITY AND CONTROL OF POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume the reservation on the part of the Chair relates to the possibility that if this amendment should be carried it would result in a charge on the federal treasury, which is something a private member cannot impose. I have two comments to make. The first is that the amendment does not in fact require a fund out of which a person may recover. The amendment asks that a study be made with reference to the feasibility of establishing a fund. This is the sort of thing I feel is most important in this piece of legislation.
The general intent of the legislation is to improve our air quality and to arrive at a means by which this might be done. I think one of the most important steps that could be taken would be to have an on-going study of a subject that has been completely left out of this legislation; it has been entirely ignored. I refer to the question of setting up a fund for compensation to persons who may be injured as a result of air pollution. The proposal says merely that the Governor in Council can cause a study to be made. I feel this is by no means necessarily a charge on the federal treasury.
The second reason is related to the first. This provision has been allowed under various other clauses. I refer particularly to motion No. 6, which was accepted as an amendment, which would permit the minister to establish a commission of inquiry for the purpose of conducting a public hearing at which the ambient air quality objectives and the national emission standards shall be
June 21, 1971

reviewed. II it is in order under motion No. 6, to set up a commission of inquiry, surely it is in order under motion No. 12 to cause a study to be made. I can see no reason for any differential between the two amendments.
If we were referring to another piece of legislation it would be difficult to refer to other situations and circumstances as precedents. But we have today accepted an almost identical amendment, motion No. 6, and I believe it would be unfair at the very least to the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) who placed this amendment on the order paper to rule it out or order while allowing amendment No. 6 and a couple of others along the same line. I do not think this would necessarily result in a charge to the treasury. It is certainly a desirable and relevant part of the whole bill. For that reason I urge Your Honour to accept the amendment and I think we could dispose of it very quickly.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: CLEAN AIR ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE RELATING TO AMBIENT AIR QUALITY AND CONTROL OF POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very briefly I should like to argue that this motion is not in order, for two reasons. First, it attempts to do indirectly what cannot be done directly by a member of this House. It asks that the Governor in Council cause a study to be made, it says very simply, only for the purpose of determining whether or not there should be a fund. I think there is another, more important reason. While the recommendation in motion No. 6 I understand did include funds for the purpose of studying the quality of air, and so on, no part of that recommendation calls for a study for the purpose of paying compensation, or indeed for establishing a fund for compensating people as called for under the provisions of amendment No. 12.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while I am sure you have taken these arguments into account, I am also sure you would agree that this motion does not meet the criteria for an amendment which is, in addition, a substantive amendment in respect of what is provided in the royal recommendation.

Order, please. The Chair is very grateful for the opinions expressed by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). I must say at the outset that I had no doubt concerning the evident financial provision contained in motion No. 12 which in my opinion would place a charge upon public funds. But I believe the point made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka is well taken, although the minister questioned it and suggested that the hon. member was trying to do indirectly what he could not do directly.
However, in respect of the other aspect of the motion which is related directly to the last point made by the minister, from the beginning the Chair has been of the opinion and has felt deeply that this motion is a substantive proposal inasmuch as it would go beyond the purport of the bill. If the hon. member wishes to look at May's Seventeenth Edition, page 549, paragraph 1, he will see that it reads:
An amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the subject matter (d) or beyond the scope of the bill (e), or if it is
Division

Amendments or new clauses creating public charges cannot be proposed-

It is the opinion of the Chair that this bill is meant to solve the problems of pollution: it is not to solve the problems of compensation. On this point alone the Chair cannot accept the motion.

WHEREAS science and technology vitally affects the well-being of Canadians and the future of Canadian society as a whole;
AND WHEREAS many of the policies and programs of the Government of Canada substantially influence directly and indirectly the development of science and technology in Canada;
AND WHEREAS the close cooperation of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is required to ensure that the development and use of science and technology advances in a manner beneficial to all Canadians;
AND WHEREAS the need for policies directed towards the most effective use of science and technology in the achievement of Canada's national goals has become increasingly urgent;
AND WHEREAS it appears to the Governor in Council that the requirements for formulating and developing such policies warrant the establishment of a special portion of the public service presided over by a minister charged with that responsibility.
NOW THEREFORE His Excellency, the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, pursuant to sections 14 and 15 of the Ministries and Ministers of State Act, is pleased to direct that a proclamation do issue establishing a Ministry of State for the purpose of formulating and developing policies in relation to the activities of the Government of Canada that affect the development and application of science and technology, to be known as the Ministry of State for Science and Technology and to be presided over by a Minister of State to be known as the Minister of State for Science and Technology.
HIS EXCELLENCY IN COUNCIL is further pleased to specify that the Minister of State for Science and Technology shall formulate and develop policies with respect to
(a)	the most appropriate means by which the Government of Canada may, through measures within its fields of jurisdiction, have a beneficial influence on
the application and development of science and technology in Canada,
(b)	the co-ordination of programs and activities regarding science and technology with other policies and programs of the Government of Canada, and
(c)	the fostering of cooperative relationships with respect to science and technology with the provinces, with public and private organizations, and with other nations.
HIS EXCELLENCY IN COUNCIL is further pleased to specify that the Minister of State for Science and Technology shall, in relation to the formulation and development of the aforementioned policies, have such duties as may be assigned to him by law, and without limiting the generality of the foregoing, shall assist departments and agencies of the Government of Canada in the formulation and development of advice to the Governor in Council with regard to
(a)	the optimum investment in, and application of, science and technology in pursuit of national objectives,
(b)	the organization of the scientific establishment in the public service of Canada,
(c)	the allocation of financial, personnel and other resources to Canadian scientific endeavours, and
(d)	the extent and nature of Canada's participation in international scientific activities and the co-ordination of related domestic activites.
HIS EXCELLENCY IN COUNCIL is further pleased to specify that the Minister of State for Science and Technology may
(a)	initiate and undertake such research, analysis and policy studies as may be required to further knowledge and understanding of the impact of science and technology on society, and
(b)	determine and promote the use of methods for assessing the effectiveness of scientific policies and programs.
Tuesday, June 22, 1971
